Cancer is a broad class of diseases characterized by uncontrolled or abnormal cell growth, where cells divide out of control due to genetic changes, and can invade nearby tissues, spread, and harm the body. This condition can affect various parts of the body, may run in families, and encompasses many specific types, including chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, and breast cancer, among others. Blood Tests are laboratory procedures performed on samples of blood to evaluate a patient’s overall health, detect abnormalities, and assess organ function. These medical tests are frequently documented in medical records and binders, serving as a foundational tool for diagnosing and monitoring a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. By analyzing blood components and chemicals, these tests can reveal signs of disease, measure how well organs are working, and identify specific markers or irregularities that guide clinical decision-making.

In the context of oncology, Blood Tests play a critical role across multiple cancer types. They are routine in cases of small cell lung cancer (SCLC), where results may be abnormal, and are integral to the diagnostic workup for esophageal cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma, and follicular lymphoma, where results help guide treatment plans. For suspected ovarian cancer, tests typically include a complete blood count (CBC), chemistry profile, liver function tests, and tumor marker tests. Similarly, for pancreatic cancer, these tests aid in diagnosis and management, while for primary CNS lymphoma, they help assess the condition. In leukemias like acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), blood tests are used to diagnose, monitor, and direct treatment strategies. For thyroid cancer, they measure specific substances such as TSH, thyroglobulin (Tg), and Tg antibodies to track disease status.

Beyond initial diagnosis, Blood Tests are essential for ongoing patient care. They are ordered as needed to monitor health and cancer status during chemotherapy, and they help establish the extent of cancer spread for treatment planning. Specific tests, including CBC, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, and liver function tests, are used to check for cancer recurrence and to evaluate organ function over time. Additionally, these tests are part of general health checks and are crucial for diagnosing and planning treatment for liver cancer. Overall, Blood Tests provide objective data on blood markers and health indicators, making them indispensable for detecting disease, assessing organ performance, and guiding therapeutic decisions across numerous medical scenarios.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

CT Scan, also known as Computed Tomography scan, is a medical imaging technique that uses X-rays and computer technology to create detailed images of the inside of the body. The procedure involves taking multiple X-ray images from different angles and combining them with a computer to produce detailed three-dimensional (3-D) pictures, as well as cross-sectional images of tissues, organs, and other structures. These scans are often performed with the use of a contrast agent to enhance image clarity, particularly for cancer detection and evaluation.

CT scans are widely used in oncology for detecting tumors, identifying cancer spread (metastasis), and staging diseases. They are commonly employed to image the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to check if cancer has spread to organs such as the liver, lungs, or other areas. For specific conditions, such as rectal cancer, CT scans help assess spread to chest and abdominal organs, while in colon cancer, they are used for surveillance in stages 2 and 3. Additionally, CT imaging is useful for detecting cancer spread to lymph nodes and for guiding procedures like lymph node or other biopsies.

Beyond diagnostic and staging purposes, CT scans play a critical role in treatment planning. They are used during radiation therapy simulation to obtain precise pictures of the cancer site, which aids in creating an effective treatment plan. The technique is also considered an alternative imaging method when MRI is unavailable or not recommended, as CT scans are generally faster to perform than MRI scans. Overall, CT scans are a versatile and essential tool for diagnosing abnormalities, guiding interventions, and monitoring treatment outcomes.

Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

Metastasis is the biological process by which cancer spreads from its primary, or original, site to other parts of the body. This dissemination occurs when cancer cells travel through the bloodstream or lymphatic system, enabling them to establish new tumors in distant or nearby anatomical locations. The process is a defining characteristic of advanced-stage cancer, as it marks the transition from a localized disease to a systemic one.

The specific destinations for metastatic spread vary depending on the origin of the primary cancer. Common sites of secondary tumor formation include the lymph nodes, lungs, bones, and liver. For instance, metastasis from prostate cancer defines advanced-stage disease, while bladder cancer may spread to lymph nodes, bones, liver, or lungs. In the context of kidney cancer, metastasis refers to the formation of new tumors outside the kidney itself.

Clinically, the presence of metastasis often necessitates further diagnostic procedures, such as a biopsy, to confirm the spread and guide treatment decisions. The formation of these secondary tumors is a critical factor in cancer prognosis, as it indicates that the disease has become more complex and challenging to treat.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures that are integral components of the immune and lymphatic systems, distributed throughout the body, including high concentrations in the neck, groin, armpits, and along the stomach's curvatures. They function as filters for lymph fluid, removing foreign particles, germs, and harmful cells, including cancer cells, while also producing immune cells like lymphocytes. With over 300 nodes present in the head and neck region alone, they serve as critical sites for disease surveillance and immune response.

These glands are common and clinically significant sites for cancer metastasis across numerous malignancies. Basal cell skin cancer, regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), rectal cancer, kidney cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, anal cancer, stomach cancer, and thyroid cancer can all spread to nearby lymph nodes. Additionally, they are involved in systemic diseases like leukemia, where cancer can spread outside the bloodstream, and in follicular lymphoma and B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, where tumors or malignant cell growths form within the nodes. In conditions like small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), cancer cells may accumulate in these organs.

Lymph nodes are routinely evaluated in cancer staging and treatment planning. Enlargement of these glands in the neck, underarm, or groin is often checked during physical exams, and they may be assessed via imaging techniques such as CT scans or MRIs. In surgical procedures like colectomy, radical cystectomy, or ovarian cancer surgery, nearby lymph nodes are often removed and tested for the presence of cancer cells. They are also targets for radiation therapy, as seen in anal cancer treatment, where beams are directed at the pelvis and groin. While they are frequent sites of metastasis for many cancers, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) does not commonly spread to these nodes.

The liver is a large organ located in the abdomen, on the right side of the body under the rib cage, and is a central component of the digestive system. It performs numerous vital functions, including filtering blood to remove toxins, producing bile to break down fats, processing nutrients and sugar for energy, synthesizing coagulation factors to aid in blood clotting, and producing lymph. A tumor is an abnormal mass or growth of tissue that arises from the uncontrolled overgrowth of cells, and it can be either benign (non-cancerous) or malignant (cancerous). Cancer Cells are abnormal cells characterized by uncontrolled growth and division, often resulting from genetic mutations or errors. Unlike normal cells, they break the standard rules of cell growth, multiply rapidly, and can avoid the natural process of cell death. These cells can crowd out and damage normal cells, leading to the formation of tumors and causing various symptoms. A defining feature of cancer cells is their ability to spread, or metastasize, to other parts of the body through the bloodstream or the lymphatic system. Lymph nodes can filter out these cells as they travel, which is a key part of how cancer spreads and is detected.

Cancer cells exhibit distinct behaviors that aid in their detection and treatment. They consume sugar at a higher rate than normal cells, causing them to appear as bright spots on PET scans, a common imaging test used for detection. Their rapid growth and spread make them targets for aggressive treatments, such as high-dose chemotherapy, which is designed to kill these dividing cells. The presence and behavior of cancer cells are central to diagnostic procedures, including imaging tests, and to the development of therapeutic strategies aimed at controlling or eliminating them.

Metastasis is the biological process by which cancer spreads from its primary, or original, site to other parts of the body. This dissemination occurs when cancer cells travel through the bloodstream or lymphatic system, enabling them to establish new tumors in distant or nearby anatomical locations. The process is a defining characteristic of advanced-stage cancer, as it marks the transition from a localized disease to a systemic one.

Hormones are chemical substances that are made in one part of the body and carried through the bloodstream to other parts of the body where they help control how organs or cells work. Each adrenal gland has 2 main parts: Adrenal cortex – This is the outer part of the adrenal gland. The adrenal cortex makes 3 main hormones: cortisol, aldosterone, and dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA). The medulla makes 3 hormones: epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine. These hormones control the body’s response to stress. This includes the “fight or flight” surge of adrenaline. These glands make hormones that help to regulate your immune system, response to stress, metabolism, and other functions. . Contrast material Contrast material is used to improve the pictures of the inside of the body. Contrast materials are not dyes, but substances that help enhance and improve the images of several organs and structures in the body. It is used to make the pictures clearer. The contrast is not permanent and will leave your body in your urine immediately after the test. The types of contrast vary and are different for CT and MRI. Tell your care team if you have had allergic reactions to contrast in the past. This is important. You might be given medicines to avoid the effects of those allergies. Contrast might not be used if you have a serious allergy or if your kidneys aren’t working well. If you smoke or vape, seek help to quit A history of smoking or vaping nicotine increases your chances of developing head and neck, lung, and other cancers. Smoking and vaping can limit how well cancer treatment works and prevent wound healing. They also greatly increase your chances of having side effects during and after surgery. Cannabis use might also affect the amount of anesthesia used during surgery. Nicotine is the chemical in tobacco that makes you want to keep smoking and vaping. Nicotine withdrawal is challenging for most people who smoke or vape. The stress of having cancer may make it even harder to quit. If you smoke or vape, ask your care team about counseling and medicines to help you quit. In head and neck cancers, stopping smoking or vaping is essential to maximize the chance for cure and minimize side effects. It takes many x-rays of the same body part from different angles. All the images are combined to make one detailed picture. A CT scan of your head, neck, and chest may be one of the tests to look for cancer. In most cases, contrast will be used. MRI scan A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. It does not use -rays. Because of the very strong magnets used in the MRI machine, tell the technologist if you have any metal in your body. During the test, you will likely be asked to hold your breath for 10 to 20 seconds as the technician collects the images. Contrast is often used. A closed MRI has a capsule-like design where the magnet surrounds you. An open MRI has a magnetic top and bottom, which allows for an opening on each end. Closed MRIs are more common than open MRIs, so if you have claustrophobia (a dread or fear of enclosed spaces), be sure to talk to your care team about it. PET scan A positron emission tomography (PET) scan uses a radioactive drug called a tracer. A tracer is a substance injected into a vein to see where cancer cells are in the body and if they are using sugar produced by your body to grow. Cancer cells show up as bright spots on PET scans. However, not all tumors will appear on a PET scan. Also, not all bright spots are cancer. It is normal for the brain, heart, kidneys, and bladder to be bright on PET. Inflammation or infection can also show up as a bright spot. When a PET scan is combined with CT, it is called a PET/CT scan. entities.description: The most common type of skin cancer, also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC), which is highly treatable and curable, especially when caught early.<SEP>A type of skin cancer that can recur at the original site or metastasize to lymph nodes or distant parts of the body.

Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

A very common type of skin cancer, occurring more often in lighter-skinned people, commonly on sun-exposed areas, rarely spreads but can be severe if untreated.<SEP>A type of skin cancer (CSCC) that can be treated with surgery, radiation therapy, and systemic therapy.

Radiation therapy is a medical treatment that uses high-energy radiation, such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons, to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is a localized treatment, meaning it affects a specific area of the body. The therapy is typically administered in daily sessions over several weeks, with each session lasting between 30 and 60 minutes, and is often used alone or in combination with other treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, or systemic therapy.

This treatment is applied to a wide range of cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), prostate cancer (both early and advanced stages), primary CNS lymphoma (including in the eyes, via whole-brain radiation therapy or focused eye treatment), chordoma, glioma, and anal cancer. For some cancers, such as anal cancer, it is a primary initial treatment, often combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation). In other cases, it is recommended when surgery is not an option, as an adjuvant therapy after surgery, or as a main treatment for unresectable tumors.

While effective, radiation therapy carries potential side effects. Short-term effects can include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, and tiredness. Long-term or late-onset side effects may include vision problems, cataracts, damage to the perineum, and effects on endocrine glands and hearing when treating the head and neck. It can also cause infertility. Furthermore, prior exposure to radiation therapy is a known risk factor for developing small cell lung cancer (SCLC). The specific delivery methods include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and brachytherapy.

Squamous Cell Skin Cancer, also referred to as CSCC, is a type of cancer that arises from squamous cells in the skin. It is the second most common form of skin cancer and is highly treatable, particularly when detected early. The condition is most often caused by cumulative sun exposure, and it can also develop in areas of skin that have been damaged by ultraviolet radiation. In addition to sun-damaged skin, CSCC can form in scars, chronic wounds, old burns, or other areas of prior skin injury; cases arising in such contexts may be more challenging to treat.

The disease has the potential to spread, or metastasize, to lymph nodes and other parts of the body, which underscores the importance of timely intervention. Treatment options for squamous cell skin cancer include topical therapies and surgical removal, with the choice of approach depending on the lesion's characteristics and location. The condition encompasses various subtypes, and risk factors—such as history of skin damage or chronic inflammation—are important considerations in its development and management. Overall, while CSCC is a serious malignancy, its prognosis is generally favorable with appropriate and prompt care.

These resources cover a wide range of cancer types, including squamous cell skin cancer, melanoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), rectal cancer, anal cancer, bone cancer, and certain lymphomas, as well as topics like adolescent and young adult cancer. The guidelines aim to empower patients to make informed, shared decisions with their care team by clearly explaining their treatment options and what to expect.

The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are accessible in multiple formats, including online at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and through the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. They are also available as printed books. The NCCN encourages users to provide feedback through surveys to help improve the guidelines. Overall, these guidelines serve as a vital educational resource, bridging the gap between complex medical information and patient understanding, ensuring individuals are well-informed participants in their own cancer care journey.

Imaging refers to a broad range of diagnostic techniques and tests that create detailed pictures of the inside of the body, used primarily to detect, stage, and monitor various cancers and other conditions. These techniques include computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), PET/CT, ultrasound, and X-rays, among others. In oncology, imaging is essential for finding tumors, such as adrenal tumors, and for visualizing internal structures like the brain, bladder, and surrounding tissues to assess tumor size, location, and spread.

Specifically, imaging plays a critical role in cancer staging, helping to determine the extent of disease and whether surgery is a viable option, as seen in pancreatic cancer and other malignancies. For certain cancers, such as locally advanced cervical cancer, imaging techniques like CT, MRI, PET, and transvaginal ultrasound are used to identify lymph node involvement and detect recurrence or spread. Additionally, imaging is employed to monitor cancer response during chemotherapy and to guide surveillance after treatment, with recommendations varying by cancer type and stage. For example, in anal cancer, yearly imaging for three years is advised for stage II and III cases, while post-recurrence treatment may involve regular CT or MRI scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Overall, imaging is a cornerstone of modern medical diagnosis and management, providing objective, non-invasive visualization to guide clinical decisions across multiple disease contexts.

Histology is the branch of biology and medicine concerned with the study of the microscopic structure of tissues, including their cells and anatomy, as well as the structure of organs under a microscope. In clinical practice, histology involves the detailed review of the appearance and cellular composition of tissue samples. This discipline is fundamental to pathology, where it is used to classify cancer subtypes—such as renal cell carcinoma (RCC)—by examining tissue under a microscope. Additionally, histology is employed to determine tumor grade and assess tumor grade, which informs prognosis and guides treatment decisions. The classification of tumors based on the microscopic appearance of cells and tissues is a core application of histology, making it essential for accurate diagnosis and therapeutic planning.

Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses drugs to kill cancer cells, typically by targeting fast-dividing or rapidly growing cells. As a systemic therapy, it works throughout the body, with drugs traveling via the bloodstream to reach cells in various locations. It is often administered intravenously, either as an infusion or injection, but can also be given orally, intraperitoneally, or directly into the bladder, depending on the cancer type. Chemotherapy is frequently delivered in cycles, allowing the body time to recover between treatments. It can be used as a primary treatment, a standard of care for certain cancers like acute myeloid leukemia (AML), primary CNS lymphoma, and high-grade gliomas, or as part of a combined approach with other therapies, such as radiation (chemoradiation) or immune checkpoint inhibitors.

The application of chemotherapy varies by cancer type and stage. It may be given before surgery (neoadjuvant) to shrink tumors, after surgery (adjuvant) based on disease stage, or as the main treatment for advanced or metastatic cancers, including ovarian, anal, prostate, and perianal cancers. For certain conditions, such as mediastinal gray zone lymphoma or anaplastic thyroid cancer, it is a common or necessary treatment, though it is not highly effective against most thyroid cancers. In stem cell rescue procedures, high-dose chemotherapy is used to destroy lymphoma cells and bone marrow stem cells. Specific drug examples include platinum-based agents like cisplatin and carboplatin, as well as capecitabine and paclitaxel.

Because chemotherapy targets all fast-dividing cells, it can also harm healthy cells, leading to side effects such as nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, hair loss, mouth sores, fever, infection, tingling or numbness, and rash. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility, as the treatment can affect fertility. Chemotherapy is considered a non-hormone therapy and is a cornerstone of systemic cancer treatment, though its effectiveness and side effects depend on the specific drugs used and the individual patient's condition.

Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of malignant cells in the ovaries, and it can also originate in the fallopian tubes. This condition encompasses various types and subtypes, including high-grade serous carcinoma and high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and is often linked to genetic factors such as germline mutations, particularly BRCA mutations, as well as Lynch syndrome. The disease may also be associated with a family history that could increase the risk of other cancers, such as prostate cancer.

Diagnosis of ovarian cancer typically involves imaging techniques and biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer cells. A notable challenge is that the disease often presents without symptoms until it reaches advanced stages, making early detection difficult. When symptoms do appear, they are discussed alongside diagnostic and treatment approaches in medical literature.

The condition is staged using a system that ranges from stage 1 to stage 4, with further substages, and treatment recommendations are based on these staging protocols. Standard treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, all of which are described in clinical guidelines. Overall, ovarian cancer is a complex disease with multiple subtypes, genetic associations, and a structured approach to diagnosis, staging, and management.

Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

Anal Cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the tissues of the anus, which includes the anal canal and the perianal region. It is an uncommon cancer of the digestive system, most often starting in the squamous cells lining the anal canal, and is frequently caused by an infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease is staged from precancerous conditions to stage IV, based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, and the presence of metastasis, and it can spread to lymph nodes and other organs. Various types of anal cancer exist, with squamous cell carcinoma being a primary form, and the condition can be either non-metastatic or metastatic.

Treatment for Anal Cancer typically involves a multidisciplinary team of digestive health experts and commonly includes chemoradiation, though surgery and immunotherapy are also viable options depending on the case. The disease has several risk factors and presents with various symptoms, and its treatment can lead to a range of side effects. Management of the disease also encompasses discussions on clinical trials and survivorship, as it is a focus of patient guidelines. While considered a rare cancer, its association with HPV and its distinct staging and treatment pathways make it a specific and serious oncological condition.

Platinum-Based Chemotherapy is a category of systemic therapy that utilizes platinum-containing drugs, such as cisplatin and carboplatin, to treat various types of cancer. This approach is frequently employed as a first-line or initial treatment for several malignancies, including ovarian cancer, where it serves as a primary therapeutic option. In the context of cervical cancer, platinum-based chemotherapy is the most commonly used systemic therapy, often applied to manage metastatic forms of the disease. Additionally, it is recommended for use in combination with radiation therapy for certain cases of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), enhancing the effectiveness of treatment. Beyond these applications, this chemotherapy class is also established as a first-line therapy for metastatic anal cancer. Overall, platinum-based regimens play a critical role across multiple cancer types, either as standalone treatments or in conjunction with other modalities like radiation, underscoring their versatility and importance in oncology.

Carboplatin is frequently employed as a therapeutic alternative to cisplatin, particularly in cases where cisplatin is considered too harsh or cannot be administered due to patient intolerance or contraindications. Cisplatin is a platinum-based chemotherapy drug used in the treatment of various cancers, including squamous cell skin cancer, cervical cancer, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. It is administered intravenously and is often combined with other medications, such as 5-FU for anal or perianal cancer, and is generally preferred for cervical cancer, where it is given weekly during chemoradiation or every three weeks for recurrent or metastatic cases. In some instances, it is used alongside other medicines if prior treatment has been received.

Cisplatin is effective but carries a range of potential side effects, including mouth sores, hair loss, fatigue, increased risk of infection, easy bleeding or bruising, nerve damage, kidney damage, tinnitus, and hearing problems. Anal Cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the tissues of the anus, which includes the anal canal and the perianal region. It is an uncommon cancer of the digestive system, most often starting in the squamous cells lining the anal canal, and is frequently caused by an infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease is staged from precancerous conditions to stage IV, based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, and the presence of metastasis, and it can spread to lymph nodes and other organs. Various types of anal cancer exist, with squamous cell carcinoma being a primary form, and the condition can be either non-metastatic or metastatic.

Treatment for Anal Cancer typically involves a multidisciplinary team of digestive health experts and commonly includes chemoradiation, though surgery and immunotherapy are also viable options depending on the case. The disease has several risk factors and presents with various symptoms, and its treatment can lead to a range of side effects. Management of the disease also encompasses discussions on clinical trials and survivorship, as it is a focus of patient guidelines. While considered a rare cancer, its association with HPV and its distinct staging and treatment pathways make it a specific and serious oncological condition.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures that are integral components of the immune and lymphatic systems, distributed throughout the body, including high concentrations in the neck, groin, armpits, and along the stomach's curvatures. Anal Cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the tissues of the anus, which includes the anal canal and the perianal region. It is an uncommon cancer of the digestive system, most often starting in the squamous cells lining the anal canal, and is frequently caused by an infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease is staged from precancerous conditions to stage IV, based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, and the presence of metastasis, and it can spread to lymph nodes and other organs. Various types of anal cancer exist, with squamous cell carcinoma being a primary form, and the condition can be either non-metastatic or metastatic.

Treatment for Anal Cancer typically involves a multidisciplinary team of digestive health experts and commonly includes chemoradiation, though surgery and immunotherapy are also viable options depending on the case. The disease has several risk factors and presents with various symptoms, and its treatment can lead to a range of side effects. Management of the disease also encompasses discussions on clinical trials and survivorship, as it is a focus of patient guidelines. While considered a rare cancer, its association with HPV and its distinct staging and treatment pathways make it a specific and serious oncological condition.

Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

Imaging Tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, diagnose, stage, and monitor a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. These tests include CT scans, MRI scans, PET scans, X-rays, ultrasound, and mammograms, among others. They are employed to visualize internal structures, locate tumors, identify swollen lymph nodes, and check for cancer spread beyond the original site. For example, they are used to detect leukemia outside the bone marrow, assess disease extent in follicular lymphoma, diagnose and stage throat cancer, and confirm liver cancer for treatment planning. In specific contexts, such as kidney cancer, tests like CT, MRI, or ultrasound are used for detection and diagnosis, while for breast cancer, mammograms, MRIs, and other techniques visualize the breast to find abnormalities. Imaging tests also play a role in determining the clinical stage of a disease, as seen with X-rays or scans, and are essential for monitoring patients with local or regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) for signs of spread. They are integral to diagnosing conditions like esophageal cancer and Hodgkin lymphoma, and are used to visualize tumors and surrounding areas for staging and treatment planning. Overall, these tests produce images of the body's interior to reveal cancer deposits, guide treatment decisions, and track disease progression.

Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of malignant cells in the ovaries, and it can also originate in the fallopian tubes. This condition encompasses various types and subtypes, including high-grade serous carcinoma and high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and is often linked to genetic factors such as germline mutations, particularly BRCA mutations, as well as Lynch syndrome. The disease may also be associated with a family history that could increase the risk of other cancers, such as prostate cancer.

Diagnosis of ovarian cancer typically involves imaging techniques and biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer cells. A notable challenge is that the disease often presents without symptoms until it reaches advanced stages, making early detection difficult. When symptoms do appear, they are discussed alongside diagnostic and treatment approaches in medical literature.

The condition is staged using a system that ranges from stage 1 to stage 4, with further substages, and treatment recommendations are based on these staging protocols. Standard treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, all of which are described in clinical guidelines. Overall, ovarian cancer is a complex disease with multiple subtypes, genetic associations, and a structured approach to diagnosis, staging, and management.

Surgery is a broad medical term for procedures that involve physical intervention, typically through an incision, to treat disease, remove cancer or other tissue, or repair the body. In oncology, it is a fundamental treatment modality used to physically remove tumors, cancerous tissue, and sometimes nearby lymph nodes. As a treatment for various cancers, its application and feasibility depend on the cancer type, stage, and location. For instance, it is the most common treatment for basal cell skin cancer and a primary treatment for early-stage cervical cancer, often involving the removal of cancerous tissue. For ovarian cancer, surgery is frequently the initial treatment, often performed by a gynecologic oncologist, and is typically followed by chemotherapy and maintenance therapy; its success depends on tumor size and location. In prostate cancer, surgery involves removing the cancerous tissue, which may include the tumor or the entire prostate, and is an option even for advanced stages. For bladder cancer, the procedure can range from removing the tumor to removing the entire bladder, depending on the stage, and may also involve removing surrounding tissue. In breast cancer, surgery is used as an initial treatment, after which pathologic staging provides more accurate details, and may involve the removal of breast tissue for analysis.

Surgery is also a key treatment for several other malignancies. It is a treatment option for early or locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and for some people with stage 1, 2, or 3 pancreatic cancer to remove cancer from the body. For thyroid cancer, it is a standard treatment involving the physical removal of tissue, with targeted therapy used when surgery cannot be performed. It is a main treatment for glioma, involving tumor removal, and can be the sole treatment for grade 1 gliomas. For chondrosarcoma and other bone cancers, surgery is used to remove tumors. In anal cancer, surgery may be used to remove the anus if the disease does not respond to treatment or returns. However, surgery is not always possible or successful, such as for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), and it is not normally an option for primary CNS lymphoma due to associated risks. Additionally, surgery may have increased side effects for smokers, and staging after the procedure provides more accurate details about the disease.

Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

Ovaries are female reproductive organs located in the pelvis, typically grape-sized, that play a central role in sexual reproduction and endocrine function. They produce eggs (oocytes) necessary for fertilization and release key hormones, including estrogen and progesterone, which regulate the menstrual cycle and support secondary sexual characteristics. These organs are integral to the female reproductive system and are the primary site where ovarian cancer originates; their size, shape, and position are routinely assessed during a pelvic exam.

Ovaries are significantly impacted by cancer treatments. Radiation therapy can damage them, potentially leading to infertility, while chemotherapy and other treatments may also affect their function, impairing both fertility and hormone production. In surgical contexts, ovaries may be removed during procedures such as ovarian cancer surgery, pelvic exenteration, or radical cystectomy if cancer has spread. During a hysterectomy, ovaries may be either removed or left in place; their removal induces surgical menopause due to the sudden loss of hormone production. Additionally, women with Lynch syndrome have an elevated risk of developing cancer in the ovaries. Overall, the ovaries are vital for reproduction and hormonal balance, and their health is a key consideration in cancer treatment planning and surgical decision-making.

Platinum-Based Chemotherapy is a category of systemic therapy that utilizes platinum-containing drugs, such as cisplatin and carboplatin, to treat various types of cancer. Treatment options for squamous cell skin cancer include topical therapies and surgical removal, with the choice of approach depending on the lesion's characteristics and location. The condition encompasses various subtypes, and risk factors—such as history of skin damage or chronic inflammation—are important considerations in its development and management. Overall, while CSCC is a serious malignancy, its prognosis is generally favorable with appropriate and prompt care.

Family History is a comprehensive record of the health information of an individual's blood relatives, including parents, siblings, children, grandparents, aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews, and half-siblings. This information encompasses the presence of various diseases and health conditions, such as heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, along with the age at which relatives were diagnosed. It serves as a critical tool in clinical practice, used to assess an individual's risk for inherited conditions and to guide healthcare decisions, treatment plans, and preventive care.

The utility of Family History is particularly pronounced in oncology. It is a key risk factor for several types of cancer, including basal cell skin cancer, prostate cancer, thyroid cancer, and bladder cancer. For instance, having a close relative (like a parent or sibling) with prostate or bladder cancer increases an individual's chance of developing the disease. Furthermore, a detailed history of cancer occurrences in family members, including the specific type of cancer and age of onset, is essential for identifying potential hereditary cancer syndromes. This information can prompt healthcare providers to recommend genetic testing and risk assessment to determine if an individual carries a higher genetic predisposition for certain malignancies, such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

These techniques include computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), PET/CT, ultrasound, and X-rays, among others. In oncology, imaging is essential for finding tumors, such as adrenal tumors, and for visualizing internal structures like the brain, bladder, and surrounding tissues to assess tumor size, location, and spread.

Specifically, imaging plays a critical role in cancer staging, helping to determine the extent of disease and whether surgery is a viable option, as seen in pancreatic cancer and other malignancies. For certain cancers, such as locally advanced cervical cancer, imaging techniques like CT, MRI, PET, and transvaginal ultrasound are used to identify lymph node involvement and detect recurrence or spread. Additionally, imaging is employed to monitor cancer response during chemotherapy and to guide surveillance after treatment, with recommendations varying by cancer type and stage. For example, in anal cancer, yearly imaging for three years is advised for stage II and III cases, while post-recurrence treatment may involve regular CT or MRI scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Overall, imaging is a cornerstone of modern medical diagnosis and management, providing objective, non-invasive visualization to guide clinical decisions across multiple disease contexts.

Radiation therapy is a medical treatment that uses high-energy radiation, such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons, to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is a localized treatment, meaning it affects a specific area of the body. The therapy is typically administered in daily sessions over several weeks, with each session lasting between 30 and 60 minutes, and is often used alone or in combination with other treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, or systemic therapy.

This treatment is applied to a wide range of cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), prostate cancer (both early and advanced stages), primary CNS lymphoma (including in the eyes, via whole-brain radiation therapy or focused eye treatment), chordoma, glioma, and anal cancer. For some cancers, such as anal cancer, it is a primary initial treatment, often combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation). In other cases, it is recommended when surgery is not an option, as an adjuvant therapy after surgery, or as a main treatment for unresectable tumors.

While effective, radiation therapy carries potential side effects. Short-term effects can include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, and tiredness. Long-term or late-onset side effects may include vision problems, cataracts, damage to the perineum, and effects on endocrine glands and hearing when treating the head and neck. It can also cause infertility. Furthermore, prior exposure to radiation therapy is a known risk factor for developing small cell lung cancer (SCLC). The specific delivery methods include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and brachytherapy.

Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of malignant cells in the ovaries, and it can also originate in the fallopian tubes. This condition encompasses various types and subtypes, including high-grade serous carcinoma and high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and is often linked to genetic factors such as germline mutations, particularly BRCA mutations, as well as Lynch syndrome. The disease may also be associated with a family history that could increase the risk of other cancers, such as prostate cancer.

Diagnosis of ovarian cancer typically involves imaging techniques and biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer cells. A notable challenge is that the disease often presents without symptoms until it reaches advanced stages, making early detection difficult. When symptoms do appear, they are discussed alongside diagnostic and treatment approaches in medical literature.

The condition is staged using a system that ranges from stage 1 to stage 4, with further substages, and treatment recommendations are based on these staging protocols. Standard treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, all of which are described in clinical guidelines. Overall, ovarian cancer is a complex disease with multiple subtypes, genetic associations, and a structured approach to diagnosis, staging, and management.

Radiation therapy is a medical treatment that uses high-energy radiation, such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons, to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is a localized treatment, meaning it affects a specific area of the body. The therapy is typically administered in daily sessions over several weeks, with each session lasting between 30 and 60 minutes, and is often used alone or in combination with other treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, or systemic therapy.

entities.description: Imaging Tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, diagnose, stage, and monitor a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. These tests include CT scans, MRI scans, PET scans, X-rays, ultrasound, and mammograms, among others. They are employed to visualize internal structures, locate tumors, identify swollen lymph nodes, and check for cancer spread beyond the original site. For example, they are used to detect leukemia outside the bone marrow, assess disease extent in follicular lymphoma, diagnose and stage throat cancer, and confirm liver cancer for treatment planning. In specific contexts, such as kidney cancer, tests like CT, MRI, or ultrasound are used for detection and diagnosis, while for breast cancer, mammograms, MRIs, and other techniques visualize the breast to find abnormalities. Imaging tests also play a role in determining the clinical stage of a disease, as seen with X-rays or scans, and are essential for monitoring patients with local or regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) for signs of spread. They are integral to diagnosing conditions like esophageal cancer and Hodgkin lymphoma, and are used to visualize tumors and surrounding areas for staging and treatment planning. Overall, these tests produce images of the body's interior to reveal cancer deposits, guide treatment decisions, and track disease progression.

Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of malignant cells in the ovaries, and it can also originate in the fallopian tubes. This condition encompasses various types and subtypes, including high-grade serous carcinoma and high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and is often linked to genetic factors such as germline mutations, particularly BRCA mutations, as well as Lynch syndrome. The disease may also be associated with a family history that could increase the risk of other cancers, such as prostate cancer.

Diagnosis of ovarian cancer typically involves imaging techniques and biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer cells. A notable challenge is that the disease often presents without symptoms until it reaches advanced stages, making early detection difficult. When symptoms do appear, they are discussed alongside diagnostic and treatment approaches in medical literature.

The condition is staged using a system that ranges from stage 1 to stage 4, with further substages, and treatment recommendations are based on these staging protocols. Standard treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, all of which are described in clinical guidelines. Overall, ovarian cancer is a complex disease with multiple subtypes, genetic associations, and a structured approach to diagnosis, staging, and management.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive medical imaging technique that uses a powerful magnet, radio waves, and a computer to create detailed, cross-sectional pictures of areas inside the body, including organs, soft tissues, bones, and internal structures. Unlike X-rays or CT scans, MRI does not use ionizing radiation, making it a safe option for repeated imaging. The technique encompasses both closed and open types of machines and can be performed with or without contrast material, which is often administered to enhance the visibility of specific tissues or abnormalities. MRI is widely used to detect, diagnose, and stage various conditions, including cancers, and is particularly valuable for examining soft tissue contrast.

In oncology, MRI plays a critical role in cancer detection, staging, and treatment planning. It is used to assess the depth of tumor invasion and lymph node involvement, notably in rectal cancer staging, and to detect cancer spread in the spine and brain. MRI is considered the most useful imaging test for identifying primary CNS lymphoma and gliomas, as it provides high-resolution images of the brain and spinal cord. For breast tissue examination, MRI helps detect abnormalities and can guide biopsies. Additionally, MRI is employed to guide applicator placement and design brachytherapy treatment plans, and it can be combined with computerized navigation systems to precisely guide biopsies. It is also used for further imaging of suspicious lymph nodes and for imaging surveillance, often with contrast, to monitor disease progression or recurrence. In some cases, MRI is combined with PET or CT to provide complementary anatomical and functional information, enhancing diagnostic accuracy across a range of clinical applications.

Ultrasound is a medical imaging technique that uses high-energy or high-frequency sound waves to create pictures of the inside of the body. It is a painless procedure that does not involve x-rays, making it safe for repeated use. The technology is versatile and can visualize various internal structures, including breast tissue, the thyroid and neck, and lymph nodes. It is often the first imaging test used for suspected ovarian cancer and is also commonly employed to evaluate and monitor thyroid nodules, as well as to guide biopsies, such as those of the prostate or lymph nodes. In specific applications, it is used in echocardiograms to examine the heart. The technique is particularly effective at showing small areas of cancer within lymph nodes and is a standard tool for guiding interventional procedures.

Anal Cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the tissues of the anus, which includes the anal canal and the perianal region. It is an uncommon cancer of the digestive system, most often starting in the squamous cells lining the anal canal, and is frequently caused by an infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease is staged from precancerous conditions to stage IV, based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, and the presence of metastasis, and it can spread to lymph nodes and other organs. Various types of anal cancer exist, with squamous cell carcinoma being a primary form, and the condition can be either non-metastatic or metastatic.

Treatment for Anal Cancer typically involves a multidisciplinary team of digestive health experts and commonly includes chemoradiation, though surgery and immunotherapy are also viable options depending on the case. The disease has several risk factors and presents with various symptoms, and its treatment can lead to a range of side effects. Management of the disease also encompasses discussions on clinical trials and survivorship, as it is a focus of patient guidelines. While considered a rare cancer, its association with HPV and its distinct staging and treatment pathways make it a specific and serious oncological condition.

Patient is an individual receiving medical care, typically within the context of a suspected or confirmed cancer diagnosis, including specific types such as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), mouth cancer, kidney cancer, breast cancer, and bone cancer. This person may be undergoing evaluation, diagnostic testing, medical imaging, and various medical procedures, and is actively engaged with a care team throughout the process. The patient may also be involved in breast cancer screening and other preventive or diagnostic measures.

In addition to receiving care, the patient is an active participant in their healthcare journey, often encouraged to advocate for themselves, ask questions, and engage in treatment planning. As someone diagnosed with cancer, the patient receives medical advice and is involved in making informed treatment decisions. Overall, the patient is the central individual undergoing tests, interacting with healthcare providers, and receiving comprehensive care tailored to their specific condition.

Clinical Trial is a form of medical research study conducted with human participants to evaluate new treatments, procedures, or interventions—including medical, surgical, and behavioral approaches—with the primary goal of determining their safety, effectiveness, and potential benefits. These studies are central to advancing cancer care, as they test investigational drugs, devices, or treatment strategies, such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies, often comparing them against standard treatments or placebos. Clinical trials are typically offered as an optional or recommended pathway for patients across various cancer types, including cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, metastatic thyroid cancer, glioma, bladder cancer, anal cancer, and metastatic anal cancer, among others. Participation may allow patients access to novel therapies while contributing to medical knowledge, and in some contexts, such as metastatic thyroid cancer or anal cancer, enrollment is strongly encouraged when trials are available.

The design and conduct of clinical trials are governed by structured protocols that include defined phases—commonly phases 2, 3, and 4—which assess treatment efficacy and safety at different stages of investigation. Trials are characterized by specific eligibility criteria, informed consent processes, and considerations regarding potential risks, benefits, and costs, though enrollment is often offered at no fee. These studies may involve placebos or investigational drugs and are conducted after laboratory development has shown promise. If a treatment proves safe and effective, it may receive approval from regulatory bodies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Clinical trials serve dual purposes: they enable patients to receive cutting-edge care and allow researchers to gather critical data on disease management, ultimately improving future treatment standards.

Clinical Trials are health research studies designed to test new ways of fighting cancer, including new treatments, therapies, and procedures. These studies investigate the safety and effectiveness of investigational treatments, with a primary focus on advancing medical care and offering hope to patients, such as those with pancreatic cancer. In the context of specific diseases, clinical trials are used to test new treatments or procedures for conditions like Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) and are being conducted in large numbers to find more targeted treatments for gliomas. Biomarker testing can determine a patient's eligibility for certain trials, and circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) testing is currently being evaluated within these research settings. By testing new therapies, clinical trials help advance treatment options for everyone, contributing to broader progress in oncology.

Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of malignant cells in the ovaries, and it can also originate in the fallopian tubes. This condition encompasses various types and subtypes, including high-grade serous carcinoma and high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and is often linked to genetic factors such as germline mutations, particularly BRCA mutations, as well as Lynch syndrome. The disease may also be associated with a family history that could increase the risk of other cancers, such as prostate cancer.

Diagnosis of ovarian cancer typically involves imaging techniques and biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer cells. A notable challenge is that the disease often presents without symptoms until it reaches advanced stages, making early detection difficult. When symptoms do appear, they are discussed alongside diagnostic and treatment approaches in medical literature.

The condition is staged using a system that ranges from stage 1 to stage 4, with further substages, and treatment recommendations are based on these staging protocols. Standard treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, all of which are described in clinical guidelines. Overall, ovarian cancer is a complex disease with multiple subtypes, genetic associations, and a structured approach to diagnosis, staging, and management.

Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

The liver is a large organ located in the abdomen, on the right side of the body under the rib cage, and is a central component of the digestive system. It performs numerous vital functions, including filtering blood to remove toxins, producing bile to break down fats, processing nutrients and sugar for energy, synthesizing coagulation factors to aid in blood clotting, and producing lymph. Its health and function are commonly assessed through blood tests, such as a chemistry profile or liver function tests, and it can be imaged using MRI to detect signs of disease.

The liver is a frequent and clinically significant site for cancer metastasis. It is a common destination for cancer cells originating from various primary tumors, including breast, colon, rectal, anal, stomach, pancreatic, cervical, bladder, kidney, prostate, throat, and nasopharyngeal cancers. In many of these cases, such as with colon cancer, the liver is a primary site for stage 4 spread, while for others, like kidney cancer, it is a less frequent but still possible site of distant metastasis. The liver can also be affected by leukemia spreading outside the bloodstream, and cancer cell buildup in the organ can cause it to swell.

Beyond its role in metastasis, the liver is susceptible to damage from certain medical treatments, such as high-dose methotrexate. As an organ that processes chemicals, its function is critical to overall health, and its assessment is a standard part of medical diagnostics.

This condition can affect various parts of the body, may run in families, and encompasses many specific types, including chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, and breast cancer, among others. Primary central nervous system lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that affects the central nervous system (CNS). Let’s break it down word by word to understand it better: Primary – Primary means first. When talking about cancer, primary refers to the place where cancer first started. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in the central nervous system. Central nervous system – The CNS is made up of the brain and spinal cord. Primary CNS lymphoma occurs more often in the brain than in the spinal cord, but it can also involve the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and/or the eyes. Lymphoma – Lymphoma is cancer that forms from lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are white blood cells that fight infections. Cancer is what happens when cells grow out of control. So, a lymphoma is an abnormal overgrowth of lymphocytes. Now let’s put it all together: Primary CNS lymphoma is a cancer that begins when lymphocytes in the brain and spinal cord grow out of control. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in lymphocytes in the immune system. The immune system is your body’s natural defense against infection and disease. Having an impaired immune system may increase the risk of developing this cancer. Primary CNS lymphoma can spread to other areas within the nervous system. For example, it may spread from the brain to the eyes. But it rarely spreads to other areas of the body. However, a different kind of lymphoma—called secondary CNS lymphoma—starts in another part of the body but then spreads to the brain or spinal cord. This book is only about primary CNS lymphoma. What is the CNS? The central nervous system (CNS) receives signals from your senses, processes information, and controls your body’s responses. The CNS includes: The brain, which controls functions of the body such as feeling, moving, thinking, and learning. The eyes are connected directly to the brain and are also part of the CNS. h The spinal cord, which transmits messages between the brain and the body. Because the CNS is so important, your body has parts that protect it. These include: Meninges, which are membranes that cover your brain and spinal cord. Cerebrospinal fluid, which is a liquid that surrounds your brain and spinal cord. h Bones including the skull that shields your brain and the vertebrae that surround your spinal cord. What causes primary CNS lymphoma? Every person diagnosed with cancer wants to know how they got it. Although no one knows exactly what causes a lymphoma, we do know that lymphomas often start with a genetic abnormality (mutation) in certain lymphocytes. This abnormality causes these lymphocytes to grow out of control (become cancerous). The abnormality occurs on its own. It’s not a mutation that occurs in other cells or organs in your body. And it’s not typically passed down in families (hereditary mutation). Although primary CNS lymphoma is rare, it could happen to almost anyone. However, some people with certain risk factors have a greater chance. Risk factors A risk factor is something that increases your chance of developing a disease. For example, having a reduced immune system increases the risk of developing primary CNS lymphoma. Lymphocytes are a type of white blood cell that forms a crucial part of the immune system, helping to fight and prevent infection and disease. They are found in the blood, lymph tissue, and throughout all organs of the body. There are three main types of lymphocytes: B lymphocytes (B cells), T lymphocytes (T cells), and natural killer cells. Lymphocytes develop from lymphoid progenitor cells and mature from lymphoblasts.

These cells are central to immune function and are also key to understanding several diseases. Lymphocytes can grow out of control and become cancerous, leading to conditions such as lymphoma, including Hodgkin lymphoma. Additionally, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) originates in lymphocytes, as this cancer starts in these white blood cells. The abnormal overgrowth of lymphocytes is directly linked to the development of lymphoma.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Performance Status is a clinical measure of a patient’s ability to perform daily activities, reflecting their overall well-being, general level of fitness, and capacity for self-care. It is commonly evaluated using standardized scales, such as the ECOG (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group) scale, which assigns a score to quantify a person’s functional capability. This assessment is widely used in cancer care, including in the context of follicular lymphoma (FL), where it informs treatment planning and helps guide therapeutic decisions. Performance Status serves as a key indicator for determining the appropriate level of treatment intensity and is also used to assess a patient’s eligibility for clinical trials. By evaluating how well a patient can manage ordinary day-to-day tasks, this metric provides clinicians with essential information to tailor care and predict a patient’s ability to tolerate specific interventions.

A condition where B-cell lymphoblasts grow mostly in lymph nodes instead of bone marrow, also called B-LL or B-LBL.<SEP>A condition where B-cell lymphoblasts grow mostly in lymph nodes instead of bone marrow.

Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures that are integral components of the immune and lymphatic systems, distributed throughout the body, including high concentrations in the neck, groin, armpits, and along the stomach's curvatures. They function as filters for lymph fluid, removing foreign particles, germs, and harmful cells, including cancer cells, while also producing immune cells like lymphocytes. With over 300 nodes present in the head and neck region alone, they serve as critical sites for disease surveillance and immune response.

These glands are common and clinically significant sites for cancer metastasis across numerous malignancies. Basal cell skin cancer, regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), rectal cancer, kidney cancer, prostate cancer, bladder cancer, anal cancer, stomach cancer, and thyroid cancer can all spread to nearby lymph nodes. Additionally, they are involved in systemic diseases like leukemia, where cancer can spread outside the bloodstream, and in follicular lymphoma and B-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma, where tumors or malignant cell growths form within the nodes. In conditions like small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), cancer cells may accumulate in these organs.

Lymph nodes are routinely evaluated in cancer staging and treatment planning. Enlargement of these glands in the neck, underarm, or groin is often checked during physical exams, and they may be assessed via imaging techniques such as CT scans or MRIs. In surgical procedures like colectomy, radical cystectomy, or ovarian cancer surgery, nearby lymph nodes are often removed and tested for the presence of cancer cells. They are also targets for radiation therapy, as seen in anal cancer treatment, where beams are directed at the pelvis and groin. While they are frequent sites of metastasis for many cancers, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) does not commonly spread to these nodes.

The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are a comprehensive set of patient-friendly guidelines published by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), a nonprofit alliance of leading cancer centers. These guidelines translate the expert consensus of the NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology into plain-language explanations, designed to help people with cancer, their families, and caregivers understand current care recommendations. The guidelines are based on the latest research and practices at leading cancer centers, providing trusted, up-to-date information on cancer treatment, testing, staging, and side effects.

These resources cover a wide range of cancer types, including squamous cell skin cancer, melanoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), rectal cancer, anal cancer, bone cancer, and certain lymphomas, as well as topics like adolescent and young adult cancer. They also address specific concerns such as immunotherapy side effects and fertility and family planning for cancer patients. The guidelines aim to empower patients to make informed, shared decisions with their care team by clearly explaining their treatment options and what to expect.

The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are accessible in multiple formats, including online at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and through the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. They are also available as printed books. The NCCN encourages users to provide feedback through surveys to help improve the guidelines. Overall, these guidelines serve as a vital educational resource, bridging the gap between complex medical information and patient understanding, ensuring individuals are well-informed participants in their own cancer care journey.
