Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

Cancer is a broad class of diseases characterized by uncontrolled or abnormal cell growth, where cells divide out of control due to genetic changes, and can invade nearby tissues, spread, and harm the body. This condition can affect various parts of the body, may run in families, and encompasses many specific types, including chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, and breast cancer, among others. Cancer presents in various stages, including metastatic and numbered stages, and can cause significant physical effects, such as bone damage, as well as emotional and psychological distress for patients. The disease can also impact fertility, often requiring medical treatment that addresses both the cancer and its side effects.

Diagnosis and management of cancer rely heavily on a range of medical techniques, including various imaging methods and biopsy procedures, which are used to detect, characterize, and monitor the disease. Treatment approaches are diverse and are discussed extensively in medical contexts, aiming to control or eliminate the abnormal cell growth. Given its complexity, cancer is a central subject of medical texts, which explore its testing, treatment, and overall impact on patients' lives.

Imaging refers to a broad range of diagnostic techniques and tests that create detailed pictures of the inside of the body, used primarily to detect, stage, and monitor various cancers and other conditions. These techniques include computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), PET/CT, ultrasound, and X-rays, among others. In oncology, imaging is essential for finding tumors, such as adrenal tumors, and for visualizing internal structures like the brain, bladder, and surrounding tissues to assess tumor size, location, and spread.

Specifically, imaging plays a critical role in cancer staging, helping to determine the extent of disease and whether surgery is a viable option, as seen in pancreatic cancer and other malignancies. For example, in anal cancer, yearly imaging for three years is advised for stage II and III cases, while post-recurrence treatment may involve regular CT or MRI scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Overall, imaging is a cornerstone of modern medical diagnosis and management, providing objective, non-invasive visualization to guide clinical decisions across multiple disease contexts.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive medical imaging technique that uses a powerful magnet, radio waves, and a computer to create detailed, cross-sectional pictures of areas inside the body, including organs, soft tissues, bones, and internal structures. Unlike X-rays or CT scans, MRI does not use ionizing radiation, making it a safe option for repeated imaging. The technique encompasses both closed and open types of machines and can be performed with or without contrast material, which is often administered to enhance the visibility of specific tissues or abnormalities. MRI is widely used to detect, diagnose, and stage various conditions, including cancers, and is particularly valuable for examining soft tissue contrast.

In oncology, MRI plays a critical role in cancer detection, staging, and treatment planning. It is used to assess the depth of tumor invasion and lymph node involvement, notably in rectal cancer staging, and to detect cancer spread in the spine and brain. MRI is considered the most useful imaging test for identifying primary CNS lymphoma and gliomas, as it provides high-resolution images of the brain and spinal cord. For breast tissue examination, MRI helps detect abnormalities and can guide biopsies. Additionally, MRI is employed to guide applicator placement and design brachytherapy treatment plans, and it can be combined with computerized navigation systems to precisely guide biopsies. It is also used for further imaging of suspicious lymph nodes and for imaging surveillance, often with contrast, to monitor disease progression or recurrence. In some cases, MRI is combined with PET or CT to provide complementary anatomical and functional information, enhancing diagnostic accuracy across a range of clinical applications.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

CT Scan, also known as Computed Tomography scan, is a medical imaging technique that uses X-rays and computer technology to create detailed images of the inside of the body. The procedure involves taking multiple X-ray images from different angles and combining them with a computer to produce detailed three-dimensional (3-D) pictures, as well as cross-sectional images of tissues, organs, and other structures. These scans are often performed with the use of a contrast agent to enhance image clarity, particularly for cancer detection and evaluation.

CT scans are widely used in oncology for detecting tumors, identifying cancer spread (metastasis), and staging diseases. They are commonly employed to image the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to check if cancer has spread to organs such as the liver, lungs, or other areas. For specific conditions, such as rectal cancer, CT scans help assess spread to chest and abdominal organs, while in colon cancer, they are used for surveillance in stages 2 and 3. Additionally, CT imaging is useful for detecting cancer spread to lymph nodes and for guiding procedures like lymph node or other biopsies.

Beyond diagnostic and staging purposes, CT scans play a critical role in treatment planning. They are used during radiation therapy simulation to obtain precise pictures of the cancer site, which aids in creating an effective treatment plan. The technique is also considered an alternative imaging method when MRI is unavailable or not recommended, as CT scans are generally faster to perform than MRI scans. Overall, CT scans are a versatile and essential tool for diagnosing abnormalities, guiding interventions, and monitoring treatment outcomes.

Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

entities.description: Cancer Stage is a medical classification that describes the extent of cancer in the body, often written with Roman numerals (e.g., I, II, III, IV). It serves as a standardized assessment of how far the cancer has likely spread from its original site, such as the ovary, and is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment plan for a patient. The staging system categorizes the disease based on whether cancer has remained localized or has metastasized; specifically, stages I, II, and III are considered non-metastatic, indicating that the cancer is confined to the primary site or has spread to nearby tissues or lymph nodes, while stage IV denotes metastatic cancer, meaning it has spread to distant organs or parts of the body. This classification provides a clear framework for healthcare providers to evaluate the severity of the disease, guide therapeutic decisions, and communicate the prognosis, ensuring that the treatment approach is tailored to the specific progression of the cancer.

Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Primary central nervous system lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that affects the central nervous system (CNS). Let’s break it down word by word to understand it better: Primary – Primary means first. When talking about cancer, primary refers to the place where cancer first started. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in the central nervous system. Central nervous system – The CNS is made up of the brain and spinal cord. Primary CNS lymphoma occurs more often in the brain than in the spinal cord, but it can also involve the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and/or the eyes. Lymphoma – Lymphoma is cancer that forms from lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are white blood cells that fight infections. Cancer is what happens when cells grow out of control. So, a lymphoma is an abnormal overgrowth of lymphocytes. Now let’s put it all together: Primary CNS lymphoma is a cancer that begins when lymphocytes in the brain and spinal cord grow out of control. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in lymphocytes in the immune system. The immune system is your body’s natural defense against infection and disease. Having an impaired immune system may increase the risk of developing this cancer. Primary CNS lymphoma can spread to other areas within the nervous system. For example, it may spread from the brain to the eyes. But it rarely spreads to other areas of the body. However, a different kind of lymphoma—called secondary CNS lymphoma—starts in another part of the body but then spreads to the brain or spinal cord. This book is only about primary CNS lymphoma. What is the CNS? The central nervous system (CNS) receives signals from your senses, processes information, and controls your body’s responses. The CNS includes: The brain, which controls functions of the body such as feeling, moving, thinking, and learning. The eyes are connected directly to the brain and are also part of the CNS. h The spinal cord, which transmits messages between the brain and the body. Because the CNS is so important, your body has parts that protect it. These include: Meninges, which are membranes that cover your brain and spinal cord. Cerebrospinal fluid, which is a liquid that surrounds your brain and spinal cord. h Bones including the skull that shields your brain and the vertebrae that surround your spinal cord. What causes primary CNS lymphoma? Every person diagnosed with cancer wants to know how they got it. Although no one knows exactly what causes a lymphoma, we do know that lymphomas often start with a genetic abnormality (mutation) in certain lymphocytes. This abnormality causes these lymphocytes to grow out of control (become cancerous). The abnormality occurs on its own. It’s not a mutation that occurs in other cells or organs in your body. And it’s not typically passed down in families (hereditary mutation). Although primary CNS lymphoma is rare, it could happen to almost anyone. However, some people with certain risk factors have a greater chance. Risk factors A risk factor is something that increases your chance of developing a disease. For example, having a reduced immune system increases the risk of developing primary CNS lymphoma. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause a disease (and just because you have risk factors, it doesn’t mean you'll definitely get the disease). But people with primary CNS lymphoma often have one or more of these risk factors: Having an immunodeficiency disorder, which is an illness that weakens the immune system’s ability to fight infections and diseases. Primary CNS lymphoma is frequently linked to HIV, the immunodeficiency virus that causes AIDS. After you’re infected, the virus remains dormant (inactive or “sleeping”) in your body for life. As the lymphoma tumor grows, it puts pressure on the CNS. This pressure often leads to neurological symptoms and difficulties, including headaches, nausea, vomiting, or seizures. Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Cancer is a broad class of diseases characterized by uncontrolled or abnormal cell growth, where cells divide out of control due to genetic changes, and can invade nearby tissues, spread, and harm the body. This condition can affect various parts of the body, may run in families, and encompasses many specific types, including chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, and breast cancer, among others. Cancer presents in various stages, including metastatic and numbered stages, and can cause significant physical effects, such as bone damage, as well as emotional and psychological distress for patients. The disease can also impact fertility, often requiring medical treatment that addresses both the cancer and its side effects.

Diagnosis and management of cancer rely heavily on a range of medical techniques, including various imaging methods and biopsy procedures, which are used to detect, characterize, and monitor the disease. Treatment approaches are diverse and are discussed extensively in medical contexts, aiming to control or eliminate the abnormal cell growth. Given its complexity, cancer is a central subject of medical texts, which explore its testing, treatment, and overall impact on patients' lives.

Smoking is the act of inhaling and exhaling smoke from tobacco products, and it is a major behavioral risk factor for numerous cancers and other diseases. Objectively, smoking is identified as the main cause of small cell lung cancer (SCLC) and the greatest risk factor for bladder cancer, accounting for about half of all cases. It also increases the risks of developing and dying from prostate cancer, and is a significant risk factor for cervical cancer, anal cancer, and cancers of the head and neck, lung, and other sites.

Beyond increasing cancer incidence, smoking adversely affects cancer treatment. It can limit the effectiveness of therapies, increase treatment-related side effects and toxicity, and impair wound healing. Consequently, smoking is a habit that negatively impacts overall treatment outcomes. Conversely, quitting smoking can lead to better cancer treatment results and reduced health risks. As a health-related behavior, smoking is generally advised to be quit, with counseling support recommended to assist individuals in overcoming the habit.

Family History is a comprehensive record of the health information of an individual's blood relatives, including parents, siblings, children, grandparents, aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews, and half-siblings. This information encompasses the presence of various diseases and health conditions, such as heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, along with the age at which relatives were diagnosed. It serves as a critical tool in clinical practice, used to assess an individual's risk for inherited conditions and to guide healthcare decisions, treatment plans, and preventive care.

The utility of Family History is particularly pronounced in oncology. It is a key risk factor for several types of cancer, including basal cell skin cancer, prostate cancer, thyroid cancer, and bladder cancer. For instance, having a close relative (like a parent or sibling) with prostate or bladder cancer increases an individual's chance of developing the disease. Furthermore, a detailed history of cancer occurrences in family members, including the specific type of cancer and age of onset, is essential for identifying potential hereditary cancer syndromes. This information can prompt healthcare providers to recommend genetic testing and risk assessment to determine if an individual carries a higher genetic predisposition for certain malignancies, such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

Primary central nervous system lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that affects the central nervous system (CNS). Let’s break it down word by word to understand it better: Primary – Primary means first. When talking about cancer, primary refers to the place where cancer first started. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in the central nervous system. Central nervous system – The CNS is made up of the brain and spinal cord. Primary CNS lymphoma occurs more often in the brain than in the spinal cord, but it can also involve the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and/or the eyes. Lymphoma – Lymphoma is cancer that forms from lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are white blood cells that fight infections. Cancer is what happens when cells grow out of control. So, a lymphoma is an abnormal overgrowth of lymphocytes. Now let’s put it all together: Primary CNS lymphoma is a cancer that begins when lymphocytes in the brain and spinal cord grow out of control. Primary CNS lymphoma starts in lymphocytes in the immune system. The immune system is your body’s natural defense against infection and disease. Having an impaired immune system may increase the risk of developing this cancer. Primary CNS lymphoma can spread to other areas within the nervous system. For example, it may spread from the brain to the eyes. But it rarely spreads to other areas of the body. However, a different kind of lymphoma—called secondary CNS lymphoma—starts in another part of the body but then spreads to the brain or spinal cord. This book is only about primary CNS lymphoma. What is the CNS? The central nervous system (CNS) receives signals from your senses, processes information, and controls your body’s responses. The CNS includes: The brain, which controls functions of the body such as feeling, moving, thinking, and learning. The eyes are connected directly to the brain and are also part of the CNS. h The spinal cord, which transmits messages between the brain and the body. Because the CNS is so important, your body has parts that protect it. These include: Meninges, which are membranes that cover your brain and spinal cord. Cerebrospinal fluid, which is a liquid that surrounds your brain and spinal cord. h Bones including the skull that shields your brain and the vertebrae that surround your spinal cord. What causes primary CNS lymphoma? Every person diagnosed with cancer wants to know how they got it. Although no one knows exactly what causes a lymphoma, we do know that lymphomas often start with a genetic abnormality (mutation) in certain lymphocytes. This abnormality causes these lymphocytes to grow out of control (become cancerous). The abnormality occurs on its own. It’s not a mutation that occurs in other cells or organs in your body. And it’s not typically passed down in families (hereditary mutation). Although primary CNS lymphoma is rare, it could happen to almost anyone. However, some people with certain risk factors have a greater chance. Risk factors A risk factor is something that increases your chance of developing a disease. For example, having a reduced immune system increases the risk of developing primary CNS lymphoma. Risk factors don’t necessarily cause a disease (and just because you have risk factors, it doesn’t mean you'll definitely get the disease). Primary CNS lymphoma is frequently linked to HIV, the immunodeficiency virus that causes AIDS. After you’re infected, the virus remains dormant (inactive or “sleeping”) in your body for life. Having an autoimmune disease, such as lupus, in which the immune system overreacts and attacks healthy tissues and organs. The most common location is in the central part of the brain. A lymphoma located here may cause specific nerve changes such as leg or arm weakness, or problems with coordination or movement. Clinical Trial is a form of medical research study conducted with human participants to evaluate new treatments, procedures, or interventions—including medical, surgical, and behavioral approaches—with the primary goal of determining their safety, effectiveness, and potential benefits. These studies are central to advancing cancer care, as they test investigational drugs, devices, or treatment strategies, such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies, often comparing them against standard treatments or placebos. Clinical trials are typically offered as an optional or recommended pathway for patients across various cancer types, including cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, metastatic thyroid cancer, glioma, bladder cancer, anal cancer, and metastatic anal cancer, among others. Participation may allow patients access to novel therapies while contributing to medical knowledge, and in some contexts, such as metastatic thyroid cancer or anal cancer, enrollment is strongly encouraged when trials are available.

The design and conduct of clinical trials are governed by structured protocols that include defined phases—commonly phases 2, 3, and 4—which assess treatment efficacy and safety at different stages of investigation. Trials are characterized by specific eligibility criteria, informed consent processes, and considerations regarding potential risks, benefits, and costs, though enrollment is often offered at no fee. These studies may involve placebos or investigational drugs and are conducted after laboratory development has shown promise. If a treatment proves safe and effective, it may receive approval from regulatory bodies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Clinical trials serve dual purposes: they enable patients to receive cutting-edge care and allow researchers to gather critical data on disease management, ultimately improving future treatment standards.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Immunotherapy is a form of cancer treatment that leverages the body's own immune system to identify, target, and destroy cancer cells. It is classified as a systemic therapy, meaning it works throughout the body, and functions by either stimulating or re-activating the immune system's natural defenses against tumors. This approach can be administered alone or in combination with other treatments, and its application spans various cancer types, including recurrent ovarian cancer, advanced-stage prostate cancer, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer, metastatic thyroid cancer, and primary CNS lymphoma, where the monoclonal antibody rituximab is a key agent.

A prominent and often preferred method within immunotherapy involves the use of immune checkpoint inhibitors, which include drugs that target proteins such as PD-1 and PD-L1. A specific example of this class is pembrolizumab. These inhibitors are frequently utilized in clinical practice, particularly for cancers like metastatic anal cancer, where they serve as a primary treatment or are recommended when the disease progresses during or after chemotherapy. In some cases, such as progressive anal cancer, these inhibitors may be administered before surgery. Additionally, immunotherapy can be delivered directly into the bladder for certain malignancies.

The application of immunotherapy is sometimes guided by the presence of specific biomarkers to determine patient eligibility. While it offers a powerful mechanism for fighting cancer, it is not without side effects. Potential adverse reactions include autoimmune responses, fatigue, fever, nausea, loss of appetite, infection, diarrhea, and constipation. Overall, immunotherapy represents a versatile and increasingly central strategy in oncology, offering options for both early and advanced-stage diseases across a wide spectrum of cancer types.

Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.
A type of cancer that affects the central nervous system, specifically the brain and spinal cord.

Bladder cancer is a disease that occurs when cells in the inner lining of the bladder grow out of control. The bladder is a hollow, balloonlike organ that stores urine. It’s located in your pelvis—the area between your hip bones in your lower abdomen. The bladder’s inner lining, called the urothelium, prevents urine from leaking back into the body. What does the bladder do? • The bladder is a hollow organ in the lower pelvis. Its main job is to store urine (pee). In adults, the bladder can hold up to 2 cups of urine. • Urine is made by the kidneys and flows down to the bladder through two tubes called ureters. • The bladder gets bigger as it fills with urine and gets smaller when you pee. It’s about the size of an orange when empty and the size of a grapefruit when full. When you urinate, the muscles in the walls of the bladder contract. This forces the urine out of the bladder and through a tube called the urethra, which streams it out of the body. • Together, these organs are called the urinary tract. Bladder cancer happens when abnormal (cancer) cells develop genetic errors (mutations) that cause them to make many more cancer cells. Cancer cells also avoid normal cell death. As cancer cells increase, they crowd out and overwhelm normal cells. Over time, the cancer cells may form a tumor in the bladder. Sometimes the cells grow deeper and invade the bladder’s muscle layer. The cancer may even break through the bladder and spread to other parts of the body. Is bladder cancer common? Bladder cancer is one of the most common cancers in adults. Most people who have bladder cancer are aged 55 years and over. Bladder cancer is often found at an early stage when the cancer is highly treatable. However, bladder cancer commonly comes back again even after treatment. In many cases, bladder cancer comes back in a different place and sometimes more advanced than before. That’s why follow-up testing is so important. People with bladder cancer need regular follow-up tests for many years to check if the cancer has returned. The most common kind of bladder cancer starts in the urothelial cells, which are stretchy cells that line the inside of the bladder. Urothelial cells also form the inner layer in the rest of the urinary tract, which includes the kidneys, the ureters, and the urethra. Cancer of the urothelium can start in these areas instead of the bladder, although it’s less common. Other (non-urothelial) types of bladder cancer are much less common. entities.description: The bladder is a hollow, balloonlike organ located in the pelvis that stores urine until it is released from the body. In adults, it can hold up to 2 cups of urine. It is part of the urinary tract, situated near the prostate in males and near the cervix in females. The bladder normally appears bright on PET scans and is involved in the excretion of contrast material used in imaging studies. It may be affected by radiation therapy, particularly when treating nearby pelvic structures, and can be invaded by advanced anal tumors (stage IIIB). The bladder is also a key site for cancer, with bladder cancer originating in its lining. It is examined during cystoscopy and imaging for signs of malignancy, and it may be removed during radical cystectomy for bladder cancer or as part of pelvic exenteration.

Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

The colon, also known as the large intestine, is a crucial part of the digestive tract and the digestive system. It is the first and longest section of the large bowel, playing a primary role in the final stages of digestion. Functionally, the colon is responsible for absorbing water from digested food, a process that transforms the remaining material into solid stool. It is the specific part of the large intestine where digested food becomes stool.

Anatomically, the colon is the segment of the large intestine that may be surgically connected to the abdominal wall in a procedure called a colostomy. This connection allows for the diversion of waste when normal bowel function is compromised.

Medically, the colon is a significant site for disease, particularly colon cancer. It is the part of the large intestine where this cancer typically develops. Furthermore, cancer originating in the colon can spread (metastasize) to other organs, most notably the liver, making it a critical area for oncological monitoring and treatment.

Colon cancer is a disease characterized by the growth of malignant cells in the colon, a part of the large intestine. It is a distinct form of cancer with treatment approaches that differ from those used for rectal cancer. The disease commonly originates from polyps, particularly adenomatous polyps, which are abnormal growths on the inner lining of the colon that can become cancerous over time. Colon cancer is considered a common and treatable form of cancer, especially when detected early, and it can present in various stages, including stages 1, 2, and 3, as well as in non-metastatic or metastatic forms.

The condition may be linked to family history, suggesting a potential genetic or hereditary component that can increase an individual's risk. Additionally, research indicates that having colon cancer may be associated with an elevated risk of developing prostate cancer. As a disease, colon cancer involves the uncontrolled division of abnormal cells within the colon, and its progression and severity are typically classified by staging systems that help guide prognosis and treatment decisions.

The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

The liver is a large organ located in the abdomen, on the right side of the body under the rib cage, and is a central component of the digestive system. It performs numerous vital functions, including filtering blood to remove toxins, producing bile to break down fats, processing nutrients and sugar for energy, synthesizing coagulation factors to aid in blood clotting, and producing lymph. Its health and function are commonly assessed through blood tests, such as a chemistry profile or liver function tests, and it can be imaged using MRI to detect signs of disease.

The liver is a frequent and clinically significant site for cancer metastasis. It is a common destination for cancer cells originating from various primary tumors, including breast, colon, rectal, anal, stomach, pancreatic, cervical, bladder, kidney, prostate, throat, and nasopharyngeal cancers. In many of these cases, such as with colon cancer, the liver is a primary site for stage 4 spread, while for others, like kidney cancer, it is a less frequent but still possible site of distant metastasis. The liver can also be affected by leukemia spreading outside the bloodstream, and cancer cell buildup in the organ can cause it to swell.

Beyond its role in metastasis, the liver is susceptible to damage from certain medical treatments, such as high-dose methotrexate. As an organ that processes chemicals, its function is critical to overall health, and its assessment is a standard part of medical diagnostics.

Imaging refers to a broad range of diagnostic techniques and tests that create detailed pictures of the inside of the body, used primarily to detect, stage, and monitor various cancers and other conditions. These techniques include computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), PET/CT, ultrasound, and X-rays, among others. In oncology, imaging is essential for finding tumors, such as adrenal tumors, and for visualizing internal structures like the brain, bladder, and surrounding tissues to assess tumor size, location, and spread.

Specifically, imaging plays a critical role in cancer staging, helping to determine the extent of disease and whether surgery is a viable option, as seen in pancreatic cancer and other malignancies. For certain cancers, such as locally advanced cervical cancer, imaging techniques like CT, MRI, PET, and transvaginal ultrasound are used to identify lymph node involvement and detect recurrence or spread. Additionally, imaging is employed to monitor cancer response during chemotherapy and to guide surveillance after treatment, with recommendations varying by cancer type and stage. For example, in anal cancer, yearly imaging for three years is advised for stage II and III cases, while post-recurrence treatment may involve regular CT or MRI scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Overall, imaging is a cornerstone of modern medical diagnosis and management, providing objective, non-invasive visualization to guide clinical decisions across multiple disease contexts.

Cancer Stage is a medical classification that describes the extent of cancer in the body, often written with Roman numerals (e.g., I, II, III, IV). It serves as a standardized assessment of how far the cancer has likely spread from its original site, such as the ovary, and is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment plan for a patient. The staging system categorizes the disease based on whether cancer has remained localized or has metastasized; specifically, stages I, II, and III are considered non-metastatic, indicating that the cancer is confined to the primary site or has spread to nearby tissues or lymph nodes, while stage IV denotes metastatic cancer, meaning it has spread to distant organs or parts of the body. This classification provides a clear framework for healthcare providers to evaluate the severity of the disease, guide therapeutic decisions, and communicate the prognosis, ensuring that the treatment approach is tailored to the specific progression of the cancer.

Pathologic Stage, also known as surgical stage or pathologic stage (p), is the stage of cancer determined by examining tissue removed during a surgical procedure. This assessment is performed after the surgery has taken place, distinguishing it from clinical staging, which is based on examinations conducted before treatment. The pathologic stage is widely regarded as providing the most accurate picture of the disease's extent, as it is based on direct analysis of the actual removed tissue rather than imaging or physical exams alone.

This staging method offers more precise and detailed information regarding key prognostic factors, particularly the size of the primary tumor and the status of lymph nodes. By evaluating the tissue excised during operations such as lymph node removal, physicians can determine the exact degree of cancer spread. Consequently, the pathologic stage serves as a critical prognostic stage, informing treatment decisions and providing a more reliable basis for predicting patient outcomes than other staging methods.

The lymphatic system is part of your immune system. It helps your body fight infection and disease. The tissues and organs that make up the lymphatic system are described next. They are made mostly of lymphocytes. There are other types of white blood cells, but lymphocytes are the most important to understanding Hodgkin lymphoma. Lymph and lymphatic vessels There is a super-highway of ducts running through your body. These ducts are called lymphatic vessels. Much like how blood vessels transport blood, lymphatic vessels transport lymph. Lymph is a clear fluid that carries infection-fighting white blood cells (lymphocytes) throughout the body. It is also called lymphatic fluid. Lymph nodes While lymph travels throughout your body in lymphatic vessels, it passes through hundreds of small bean-shaped structures called lymph nodes. Lymph nodes catch and filter out foreign particles and harmful cells, including cancer cells. Lymph nodes can’t usually be seen or felt. The highest numbers of lymph nodes are found in the neck, groin, and armpits. Spleen The spleen is the largest organ of the lymphatic system. It is about 4 inches long and shaped like a fist. It makes lymphocytes and plays an important role in blood filtration and storage. Lymphatic system There are hundreds of small bean-shaped structures, called lymph nodes, throughout the human body. They catch and filter out foreign particles and harmful cells, including cancer cells. Bone marrow Most bones have soft, spongy tissue in the center called bone marrow. This is where new blood cells are made. Thymus After being made in bone marrow, lymphocytes travel to the thymus. The thymus is a small organ in the upper chest. Here lymphocytes develop into T lymphocytes (T cells), one of the two main types of lymphocytes. The tonsils Tonsils are small masses of lymph tissue found at the back of the throat. They help trap disease-causing germs that enter through you nose or mouth. Types of Hodgkin lymphoma There are 2 types of Hodgkin lymphoma, described next. Classic Hodgkin lymphoma Most people with Hodgkin lymphoma have classic Hodgkin lymphoma (CHL). CHL can be recognized by large lymphocytes called ReedSternberg cells. While there are different subtypes of CHL, the same care is recommended for all of them. NLPHL While CHL is known for Reed-Sternberg cells, nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (NLPHL) is known for popcornshaped cells. This rare form of Hodgkin lymphoma usually grows slowly, but in rare cases behaves aggressively. Over time, it can transform into one of several types of fast-growing cancer, including diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). What can you do to get the best care? Advocate for yourself. entities.description: Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

Imaging Tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, diagnose, stage, and monitor a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. These tests include CT scans, MRI scans, PET scans, X-rays, ultrasound, and mammograms, among others. They are employed to visualize internal structures, locate tumors, identify swollen lymph nodes, and check for cancer spread beyond the original site. For example, they are used to detect leukemia outside the bone marrow, assess disease extent in follicular lymphoma, diagnose and stage throat cancer, and confirm liver cancer for treatment planning. In specific contexts, such as kidney cancer, tests like CT, MRI, or ultrasound are used for detection and diagnosis, while for breast cancer, mammograms, MRIs, and other techniques visualize the breast to find abnormalities. Imaging tests also play a role in determining the clinical stage of a disease, as seen with X-rays or scans, and are essential for monitoring patients with local or regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) for signs of spread. They are integral to diagnosing conditions like esophageal cancer and Hodgkin lymphoma, and are used to visualize tumors and surrounding areas for staging and treatment planning. Overall, these tests produce images of the body's interior to reveal cancer deposits, guide treatment decisions, and track disease progression.

Blood Tests are laboratory procedures performed on samples of blood to evaluate a patient’s overall health, detect abnormalities, and assess organ function. These medical tests are frequently documented in medical records and binders, serving as a foundational tool for diagnosing and monitoring a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. By analyzing blood components and chemicals, these tests can reveal signs of disease, measure how well organs are working, and identify specific markers or irregularities that guide clinical decision-making.

In the context of oncology, Blood Tests play a critical role across multiple cancer types. They are routine in cases of small cell lung cancer (SCLC), where results may be abnormal, and are integral to the diagnostic workup for esophageal cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma, and follicular lymphoma, where results help guide treatment plans. For suspected ovarian cancer, tests typically include a complete blood count (CBC), chemistry profile, liver function tests, and tumor marker tests. Similarly, for pancreatic cancer, these tests aid in diagnosis and management, while for primary CNS lymphoma, they help assess the condition. In leukemias like acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), blood tests are used to diagnose, monitor, and direct treatment strategies. For thyroid cancer, they measure specific substances such as TSH, thyroglobulin (Tg), and Tg antibodies to track disease status.

Beyond initial diagnosis, Blood Tests are essential for ongoing patient care. They are ordered as needed to monitor health and cancer status during chemotherapy, and they help establish the extent of cancer spread for treatment planning. Specific tests, including CBC, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, and liver function tests, are used to check for cancer recurrence and to evaluate organ function over time. Additionally, these tests are part of general health checks and are crucial for diagnosing and planning treatment for liver cancer. Overall, Blood Tests provide objective data on blood markers and health indicators, making them indispensable for detecting disease, assessing organ performance, and guiding therapeutic decisions across numerous medical scenarios.

The Lymphatic System is a major part of the body’s immune system, functioning as a network of tissues, organs, and vessels that helps the body fight infection and disease. It is composed primarily of lymphocytes and includes key structures such as lymph nodes, the spleen, bone marrow, thymus, tonsils, and lymphatic vessels. This system also serves as a network that carries lymph—a clear fluid containing white blood cells—throughout the body, helping to circulate immune cells and defend against germs. Additionally, the lymphatic system plays a role in ridding the body of toxins and waste. Because it transports lymph fluid, cancer cells can spread through this system to other parts of the body. Overall, it is essential for immune defense, fluid balance, and waste removal.

Lymphocytes are a type of white blood cell that forms a crucial part of the immune system, helping to fight and prevent infection and disease. They are found in the blood, lymph tissue, and throughout all organs of the body. There are three main types of lymphocytes: B lymphocytes (B cells), T lymphocytes (T cells), and natural killer cells. Lymphocytes develop from lymphoid progenitor cells and mature from lymphoblasts.

These cells are central to immune function and are also key to understanding several diseases. Lymphocytes can grow out of control and become cancerous, leading to conditions such as lymphoma, including Hodgkin lymphoma. Additionally, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) originates in lymphocytes, as this cancer starts in these white blood cells. The abnormal overgrowth of lymphocytes is directly linked to the development of lymphoma.

The lymphatic system is part of your immune system. It helps your body fight infection and disease. The tissues and organs that make up the lymphatic system are described next. Lymph and lymphatic vessels There is a super-highway of ducts running through your body. These ducts are called lymphatic vessels. Much like how blood vessels transport blood, lymphatic vessels transport lymph. Lymph is a clear fluid that carries infection-fighting white blood cells (lymphocytes) throughout the body. It is also called lymphatic fluid. Lymph nodes While lymph travels throughout your body in lymphatic vessels, it passes through hundreds of small bean-shaped structures called lymph nodes. Lymph nodes catch and filter out foreign particles and harmful cells, including cancer cells. Lymph nodes can’t usually be seen or felt. The highest numbers of lymph nodes are found in the neck, groin, and armpits. Spleen The spleen is the largest organ of the lymphatic system. It is about 4 inches long and shaped like a fist. They catch and filter out foreign particles and harmful cells, including cancer cells. Bone marrow Most bones have soft, spongy tissue in the center called bone marrow. This is where new blood cells are made. Thymus After being made in bone marrow, lymphocytes travel to the thymus. The thymus is a small organ in the upper chest. Here lymphocytes develop into T lymphocytes (T cells), one of the two main types of lymphocytes. The tonsils Tonsils are small masses of lymph tissue found at the back of the throat. About basal cell skin cancer What is basal cell skin cancer? How is basal cell skin cancer treated? What can you do to get the best care? Basal cell skin cancer, also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC), is the most common type of skin cancer. About 3 million cases of basal cell skin cancer are diagnosed every year in the United States. The good news is it can be cured in most cases. Treatment usually involves surgery to remove the cancer. Keep reading to find out more. What is basal cell skin cancer? Basal cell skin cancer is the most common of all skin cancer types. If caught early, it is easily treatable and curable. This is because it rarely metastasizes (spreads). Skin cancers often occur in the top layer of the skin (epidermis) and less commonly in the middle layer of the skin (dermis). The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. This cancer usually develops in areas exposed to the sun, including the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk. But it can occur anywhere on the body. Skin lesions Basal cell skin cancer is often found on the face, head, and neck. Here is a basal cell lesion pictured on a person's cheek. Skin basics Did you know that your skin is your body’s largest organ and if you measured it it would stretch to about 20 square feet? Working as a barrier, your skin protects you from bacteria and chemicals and helps control your body temperature. It has 3 layers: Epidermis – The top layer of skin provides a waterproof barrier and creates skin color (melanin). Dermis – The middle layer involves connective tissue, blood vessels, oil and sweat glands, nerves, and hair follicles. Hypodermis – The deepest tissue layer is made up of fat and connective tissue. Most skin cancers form in the cells of the epidermis. It has 3 main types of cells: Squamous cells – These cells are flat cells found in the upper part of the epidermis. Basal cells – Found in the lower part of the epidermis, basal cells constantly divide to form new cells that replace the squamous cells on the skin’s surface. Melanocytes – Melanocytes are cells located in the lower part of the epidermis that produce melanin. Melanin is responsible for our hair, skin, and eye color. It also protects our skin from harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays. This book is only about basal cell skin cancer. For more information on squamous cell skin cancer or melanoma, read the NCCN Guidelines for Patients, available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. Signs and symptoms Basal cell skin cancer can happen to anyone but it’s most common in people with lighter skin, lighter hair, or lighter eyes. In lighter skin, its lesions can look like any of the following: h Flat, pale or yellow areas, like a scar h Red patches that might be itchy Small, pink or red, shiny bumps that may have blue, brown, or black areas Open sores that don’t heal and might bleed, or go away and come back In darker (brown and black) skin, basal cell skin cancer can appear as a brown or glossy black bump with a rolled border. It can be mistaken for a normal mole. Be sure to look out for any new, changing, bleeding, or unusual skin growths. Skin cancer is easier to cure when it is caught early. To find out how basal cell skin cancer is diagnosed, read Chapter 2: Testing for basal cell skin cancer. Causes and risk factors Basal cell skin cancer is caused by exposure to UV radiation from the sun or other sources like tanning beds. UV radiation can harm the DNA inside basal skin cells. DNA controls how cells grow and function. If the DNA inside cells becomes damaged, the cells can become abnormal and grow out of control. You’re more likely to have basal cell skin cancer if you have certain risk factors. A risk factor increases the chance of developing cancer. Risk factors for basal cell skin cancer include: UV light exposure – UV light (radiation) that comes from the sun or tanning beds increases your risk. Fair skin, red or blond hair, or light eye color – People with lighter-colored skin are at a higher risk of developing skin cancer because melanin (skin pigment) filters out the sun's harmful UV rays. Age – Risk increases with age because sun exposure builds up over time. But skin cancer is becoming more common in younger people. History of skin cancer – If you or someone in your family has had skin cancer, you’re more likely to develop any type of skin cancer. Radiation therapy – Radiation treatment for other conditions, especially at a young age, can cause skin cancer. Immune suppression – People with weakened immune systems from organ transplants or autoimmune diseases are at higher risk for basal cell skin cancer. How is basal cell skin cancer treated? Basal cell skin cancer is highly treatable and curable. Catching it and treating it early is key. Surgery is the most common treatment for basal cell skin cancer. In some cases, radiation therapy or systemic therapy might be used to treat it. Following your treatment, you will have full skin exams with your doctor at least once a year. Between these periods, prevention is important. See Chapter 4: Treatment by risk and recurrence for more information. Recurrence is when basal cell skin cancer returns to the area where it was originally found, or it has metastasized (spread) to the lymph nodes or to distant parts of the body. Anal Cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the tissues of the anus, which includes the anal canal and the perianal region. It is an uncommon cancer of the digestive system, most often starting in the squamous cells lining the anal canal, and is frequently caused by an infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease is staged from precancerous conditions to stage IV, based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, and the presence of metastasis, and it can spread to lymph nodes and other organs. Various types of anal cancer exist, with squamous cell carcinoma being a primary form, and the condition can be either non-metastatic or metastatic.

Treatment for Anal Cancer typically involves a multidisciplinary team of digestive health experts and commonly includes chemoradiation, though surgery and immunotherapy are also viable options depending on the case. The disease has several risk factors and presents with various symptoms, and its treatment can lead to a range of side effects. Management of the disease also encompasses discussions on clinical trials and survivorship, as it is a focus of patient guidelines. While considered a rare cancer, its association with HPV and its distinct staging and treatment pathways make it a specific and serious oncological condition.

Smoking is the act of inhaling and exhaling smoke from tobacco products, and it is a major behavioral risk factor for numerous cancers and other diseases. Objectively, smoking is identified as the main cause of small cell lung cancer (SCLC) and the greatest risk factor for bladder cancer, accounting for about half of all cases. It also increases the risks of developing and dying from prostate cancer, and is a significant risk factor for cervical cancer, anal cancer, and cancers of the head and neck, lung, and other sites.

Beyond increasing cancer incidence, smoking adversely affects cancer treatment. It can limit the effectiveness of therapies, increase treatment-related side effects and toxicity, and impair wound healing. Consequently, smoking is a habit that negatively impacts overall treatment outcomes. Conversely, quitting smoking can lead to better cancer treatment results and reduced health risks. As a health-related behavior, smoking is generally advised to be quit, with counseling support recommended to assist individuals in overcoming the habit.

Squamous Cell Skin Cancer, also referred to as CSCC, is a type of cancer that arises from squamous cells in the skin. It is the second most common form of skin cancer and is highly treatable, particularly when detected early. The condition is most often caused by cumulative sun exposure, and it can also develop in areas of skin that have been damaged by ultraviolet radiation. In addition to sun-damaged skin, CSCC can form in scars, chronic wounds, old burns, or other areas of prior skin injury; cases arising in such contexts may be more challenging to treat.

The disease has the potential to spread, or metastasize, to lymph nodes and other parts of the body, which underscores the importance of timely intervention. Treatment options for squamous cell skin cancer include topical therapies and surgical removal, with the choice of approach depending on the lesion's characteristics and location. The condition encompasses various subtypes, and risk factors—such as history of skin damage or chronic inflammation—are important considerations in its development and management. Overall, while CSCC is a serious malignancy, its prognosis is generally favorable with appropriate and prompt care.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Family History is a comprehensive record of the health information of an individual's blood relatives, including parents, siblings, children, grandparents, aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews, and half-siblings. This information encompasses the presence of various diseases and health conditions, such as heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, along with the age at which relatives were diagnosed. It serves as a critical tool in clinical practice, used to assess an individual's risk for inherited conditions and to guide healthcare decisions, treatment plans, and preventive care.

The utility of Family History is particularly pronounced in oncology. It is a key risk factor for several types of cancer, including basal cell skin cancer, prostate cancer, thyroid cancer, and bladder cancer. For instance, having a close relative (like a parent or sibling) with prostate or bladder cancer increases an individual's chance of developing the disease. Furthermore, a detailed history of cancer occurrences in family members, including the specific type of cancer and age of onset, is essential for identifying potential hereditary cancer syndromes. This information can prompt healthcare providers to recommend genetic testing and risk assessment to determine if an individual carries a higher genetic predisposition for certain malignancies, such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

entities.description: Prognosis is the likely course and outcome of a disease, such as cancer, serving as a prediction or forecast of how the condition will progress and resolve. It is a central concept in guiding treatment decisions, as it provides an expectation of the disease's trajectory and eventual result. The determination of a prognosis is informed by multiple clinical factors, including cancer staging, which helps predict the likely path of the disease. Additionally, biomarker and genetic tests are used to refine the prognosis, offering a more precise understanding of the disease's probable behavior based on the tumor's molecular characteristics. In essence, prognosis synthesizes information from staging and laboratory tests to articulate the anticipated course and outcome of the illness.

Prostate Cancer is a disease in which cells in the prostate gland grow out of control, and it is one of the most common types of cancer. The condition can be early-stage (localized) or advanced-stage (metastatic), with the latter occurring when cancer spreads outside the prostate to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes and bones, through a process called metastasis. Prostate cancer is often slow-growing and asymptomatic in its early stages, contributing to high survival rates when detected early. Risk factors for developing the disease include age, family history, genetic factors, race, and lifestyle. Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

Imaging Tests are medical procedures that create pictures of the inside of the body, used to detect, diagnose, stage, and monitor a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. These tests include CT scans, MRI scans, PET scans, X-rays, ultrasound, and mammograms, among others. They are employed to visualize internal structures, locate tumors, identify swollen lymph nodes, and check for cancer spread beyond the original site. For example, they are used to detect leukemia outside the bone marrow, assess disease extent in follicular lymphoma, diagnose and stage throat cancer, and confirm liver cancer for treatment planning. In specific contexts, such as kidney cancer, tests like CT, MRI, or ultrasound are used for detection and diagnosis, while for breast cancer, mammograms, MRIs, and other techniques visualize the breast to find abnormalities. Imaging tests also play a role in determining the clinical stage of a disease, as seen with X-rays or scans, and are essential for monitoring patients with local or regional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) for signs of spread. They are integral to diagnosing conditions like esophageal cancer and Hodgkin lymphoma, and are used to visualize tumors and surrounding areas for staging and treatment planning. Overall, these tests produce images of the body's interior to reveal cancer deposits, guide treatment decisions, and track disease progression.

Clinical Trial is a form of medical research study conducted with human participants to evaluate new treatments, procedures, or interventions—including medical, surgical, and behavioral approaches—with the primary goal of determining their safety, effectiveness, and potential benefits. These studies are central to advancing cancer care, as they test investigational drugs, devices, or treatment strategies, such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and other systemic therapies, often comparing them against standard treatments or placebos. Clinical trials are typically offered as an optional or recommended pathway for patients across various cancer types, including cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, metastatic thyroid cancer, glioma, bladder cancer, anal cancer, and metastatic anal cancer, among others. Participation may allow patients access to novel therapies while contributing to medical knowledge, and in some contexts, such as metastatic thyroid cancer or anal cancer, enrollment is strongly encouraged when trials are available.

The design and conduct of clinical trials are governed by structured protocols that include defined phases—commonly phases 2, 3, and 4—which assess treatment efficacy and safety at different stages of investigation. Trials are characterized by specific eligibility criteria, informed consent processes, and considerations regarding potential risks, benefits, and costs, though enrollment is often offered at no fee. These studies may involve placebos or investigational drugs and are conducted after laboratory development has shown promise. If a treatment proves safe and effective, it may receive approval from regulatory bodies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Clinical trials serve dual purposes: they enable patients to receive cutting-edge care and allow researchers to gather critical data on disease management, ultimately improving future treatment standards.

Basal cell skin cancer, also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC), is the most common type of skin cancer. About 3 million cases of basal cell skin cancer are diagnosed every year in the United States. The good news is it can be cured in most cases. Treatment usually involves surgery to remove the cancer. This is because it rarely metastasizes (spreads). Skin cancers often occur in the top layer of the skin (epidermis) and less commonly in the middle layer of the skin (dermis). The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. This cancer usually develops in areas exposed to the sun, including the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk. But it can occur anywhere on the body. The condition can be early-stage (localized) or advanced-stage (metastatic), with the latter occurring when cancer spreads outside the prostate to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes and bones, through a process called metastasis. Prostate cancer is often slow-growing and asymptomatic in its early stages, contributing to high survival rates when detected early. Risk factors for developing the disease include age, family history, genetic factors, race, and lifestyle. Detection and risk assessment involve various tests, including PSA (prostate-specific antigen) levels, biopsy, and grading, and the disease often requires staging and treatment. The condition is also a focus of risk assessment and genetic testing discussions, as it is characterized by the presence of prostate cancer cells and abnormal cell growth within the gland.
