Basal cell skin cancer, also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC), is the most common type of skin cancer. About 3 million cases of basal cell skin cancer are diagnosed every year in the United States. The good news is it can be cured in most cases. Treatment usually involves surgery to remove the cancer. Keep reading to find out more. What is basal cell skin cancer? Basal cell skin cancer is the most common of all skin cancer types. If caught early, it is easily treatable and curable. This is because it rarely metastasizes (spreads). Skin cancers often occur in the top layer of the skin (epidermis) and less commonly in the middle layer of the skin (dermis). The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. This cancer usually develops in areas exposed to the sun, including the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk. But it can occur anywhere on the body. Skin lesions Basal cell skin cancer is often found on the face, head, and neck. Here is a basal cell lesion pictured on a person's cheek. Skin basics Did you know that your skin is your body’s largest organ and if you measured it it would stretch to about 20 square feet? Working as a barrier, your skin protects you from bacteria and chemicals and helps control your body temperature. It has 3 layers: Epidermis – The top layer of skin provides a waterproof barrier and creates skin color (melanin). Dermis – The middle layer involves connective tissue, blood vessels, oil and sweat glands, nerves, and hair follicles. Hypodermis – The deepest tissue layer is made up of fat and connective tissue. Most skin cancers form in the cells of the epidermis. It has 3 main types of cells: Squamous cells – These cells are flat cells found in the upper part of the epidermis. Basal cells – Found in the lower part of the epidermis, basal cells constantly divide to form new cells that replace the squamous cells on the skin’s surface. Melanocytes – Melanocytes are cells located in the lower part of the epidermis that produce melanin. Melanin is responsible for our hair, skin, and eye color. It also protects our skin from harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays. This book is only about basal cell skin cancer. For more information on squamous cell skin cancer or melanoma, read the NCCN Guidelines for Patients, available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. Signs and symptoms Basal cell skin cancer can happen to anyone but it’s most common in people with lighter skin, lighter hair, or lighter eyes. In lighter skin, its lesions can look like any of the following: h Flat, pale or yellow areas, like a scar h Red patches that might be itchy Small, pink or red, shiny bumps that may have blue, brown, or black areas Open sores that don’t heal and might bleed, or go away and come back In darker (brown and black) skin, basal cell skin cancer can appear as a brown or glossy black bump with a rolled border. It can be mistaken for a normal mole. Be sure to look out for any new, changing, bleeding, or unusual skin growths. Skin cancer is easier to cure when it is caught early. To find out how basal cell skin cancer is diagnosed, read Chapter 2: Testing for basal cell skin cancer. Causes and risk factors Basal cell skin cancer is caused by exposure to UV radiation from the sun or other sources like tanning beds. UV radiation can harm the DNA inside basal skin cells. DNA controls how cells grow and function. If the DNA inside cells becomes damaged, the cells can become abnormal and grow out of control. You’re more likely to have basal cell skin cancer if you have certain risk factors. A risk factor increases the chance of developing cancer. Risk factors for basal cell skin cancer include: UV light exposure – UV light (radiation) that comes from the sun or tanning beds increases your risk. Fair skin, red or blond hair, or light eye color – People with lighter-colored skin are at a higher risk of developing skin cancer because melanin (skin pigment) filters out the sun's harmful UV rays. History of skin cancer – If you or someone in your family has had skin cancer, you’re more likely to develop any type of skin cancer. Radiation therapy is a medical treatment that uses high-energy radiation, such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons, to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is a localized treatment, meaning it affects a specific area of the body. The therapy is typically administered in daily sessions over several weeks, with each session lasting between 30 and 60 minutes, and is often used alone or in combination with other treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, or systemic therapy.

This treatment is applied to a wide range of cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), prostate cancer (both early and advanced stages), primary CNS lymphoma (including in the eyes, via whole-brain radiation therapy or focused eye treatment), chordoma, glioma, and anal cancer. For some cancers, such as anal cancer, it is a primary initial treatment, often combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation). In other cases, it is recommended when surgery is not an option, as an adjuvant therapy after surgery, or as a main treatment for unresectable tumors.

While effective, radiation therapy carries potential side effects. Short-term effects can include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, and tiredness. Long-term or late-onset side effects may include vision problems, cataracts, damage to the perineum, and effects on endocrine glands and hearing when treating the head and neck. It can also cause infertility. Furthermore, prior exposure to radiation therapy is a known risk factor for developing small cell lung cancer (SCLC). The specific delivery methods include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and brachytherapy.

Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses drugs to kill cancer cells, typically by targeting fast-dividing or rapidly growing cells. As a systemic therapy, it works throughout the body, with drugs traveling via the bloodstream to reach cells in various locations. It is often administered intravenously, either as an infusion or injection, but can also be given orally, intraperitoneally, or directly into the bladder, depending on the cancer type. Chemotherapy is frequently delivered in cycles, allowing the body time to recover between treatments. It can be used as a primary treatment, a standard of care for certain cancers like acute myeloid leukemia (AML), primary CNS lymphoma, and high-grade gliomas, or as part of a combined approach with other therapies, such as radiation (chemoradiation) or immune checkpoint inhibitors.

The application of chemotherapy varies by cancer type and stage. It may be given before surgery (neoadjuvant) to shrink tumors, after surgery (adjuvant) based on disease stage, or as the main treatment for advanced or metastatic cancers, including ovarian, anal, prostate, and perianal cancers. For certain conditions, such as mediastinal gray zone lymphoma or anaplastic thyroid cancer, it is a common or necessary treatment, though it is not highly effective against most thyroid cancers. In stem cell rescue procedures, high-dose chemotherapy is used to destroy lymphoma cells and bone marrow stem cells. Specific drug examples include platinum-based agents like cisplatin and carboplatin, as well as capecitabine and paclitaxel.

Because chemotherapy targets all fast-dividing cells, it can also harm healthy cells, leading to side effects such as nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, hair loss, mouth sores, fever, infection, tingling or numbness, and rash. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility, as the treatment can affect fertility. Chemotherapy is considered a non-hormone therapy and is a cornerstone of systemic cancer treatment, though its effectiveness and side effects depend on the specific drugs used and the individual patient's condition.

Basal cell skin cancer, also known as basal cell carcinoma (BCC), is the most common type of skin cancer. Keep reading to find out more. What is basal cell skin cancer? Basal cell skin cancer is the most common of all skin cancer types. If caught early, it is easily treatable and curable. This is because it rarely metastasizes (spreads). Skin cancers often occur in the top layer of the skin (epidermis) and less commonly in the middle layer of the skin (dermis). The epidermis is made up of basal cells and other cells. Basal cell skin cancer occurs when some basal cells become abnormal and grow out of control. This cancer usually develops in areas exposed to the sun, including the face, head, neck, arms, legs, and trunk. But it can occur anywhere on the body. Skin lesions Basal cell skin cancer is often found on the face, head, and neck. Here is a basal cell lesion pictured on a person's cheek. Skin basics Did you know that your skin is your body’s largest organ and if you measured it it would stretch to about 20 square feet? Working as a barrier, your skin protects you from bacteria and chemicals and helps control your body temperature. It has 3 layers: Epidermis – The top layer of skin provides a waterproof barrier and creates skin color (melanin). Dermis – The middle layer involves connective tissue, blood vessels, oil and sweat glands, nerves, and hair follicles. Hypodermis – The deepest tissue layer is made up of fat and connective tissue. Most skin cancers form in the cells of the epidermis. It has 3 main types of cells: Squamous cells – These cells are flat cells found in the upper part of the epidermis. Basal cells – Found in the lower part of the epidermis, basal cells constantly divide to form new cells that replace the squamous cells on the skin’s surface. Melanocytes – Melanocytes are cells located in the lower part of the epidermis that produce melanin. Melanin is responsible for our hair, skin, and eye color. It also protects our skin from harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays. This book is only about basal cell skin cancer. For more information on squamous cell skin cancer or melanoma, read the NCCN Guidelines for Patients, available at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and on the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. Signs and symptoms Basal cell skin cancer can happen to anyone but it’s most common in people with lighter skin, lighter hair, or lighter eyes. It can be mistaken for a normal mole. Be sure to look out for any new, changing, bleeding, or unusual skin growths. Skin cancer is easier to cure when it is caught early. To find out how basal cell skin cancer is diagnosed, read Chapter 2: Testing for basal cell skin cancer. Causes and risk factors Basal cell skin cancer is caused by exposure to UV radiation from the sun or other sources like tanning beds. UV radiation can harm the DNA inside basal skin cells. DNA controls how cells grow and function. If the DNA inside cells becomes damaged, the cells can become abnormal and grow out of control. You’re more likely to have basal cell skin cancer if you have certain risk factors. A risk factor increases the chance of developing cancer. Risk factors for basal cell skin cancer include: UV light exposure – UV light (radiation) that comes from the sun or tanning beds increases your risk. Fair skin, red or blond hair, or light eye color – People with lighter-colored skin are at a higher risk of developing skin cancer because melanin (skin pigment) filters out the sun's harmful UV rays. Age – Risk increases with age because sun exposure builds up over time. But skin cancer is becoming more common in younger people. Immune suppression – People with weakened immune systems from organ transplants or autoimmune diseases are at higher risk for basal cell skin cancer. How is basal cell skin cancer treated? Many diseases have signs and symptoms similar to primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma, including neurological illnesses and other types of brain cancer. So it’s important to have tests to confirm your diagnosis. If you're given a diagnosis of primary CNS lymphoma, you’ll have more tests to find out how far the cancer extends within the central nervous system or if it has spread to another area of the body. Tests are also used to help plan your treatment. Tests for diagnosis If you haven’t yet been diagnosed with primary CNS lymphoma, you’ll first have a physical examination and some general assessments of your health. These include a neurological exam and an evaluation of your level of activity. After these, you’ll have imaging scans and one or more biopsies. Neurological exam This exam involves some simple tests to check your alertness, balance, coordination, reflexes, hearing, and other senses. Your doctor may also perform an eye exam to look at the health of the nerves in the back of your eye. Performance status Your care team will want to know how well you can do ordinary day-to-day activities—like taking a walk, climbing stairs, cooking dinner, carrying laundry, or taking a bath or shower. This evaluation is called performance status. The more activities you can do, the better your performance status. Your care team uses this evaluation to get a sense of the level of treatment you may be able to handle and whether you may be eligible for a clinical trial. Imaging Imaging tests take pictures (images) of the insides of your body. The images show areas in the body that might have cancer. The images can reveal a lymphoma’s location, size, and other features. MRI Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the most useful imaging technique for identifying primary CNS lymphoma. An MRI scan is good at showing the spine and soft tissues, including the brain, as well as other details that are helpful for planning surgery. MRI uses radio waves and powerful magnets to take pictures of the inside of the body. During an MRI, you’ll lie on a table that slides into the scanning machine. (An open MRI scanner may be an option at some health care centers.) It’s important to lie still during the test to get the best pictures. The machine makes loud noises but you can wear earplugs. An MRI of the brain or spinal cord usually requires a contrast agent (also called contrast dye or just contrast). Contrast highlights areas in organs, blood vessels, or other tissues to make them easier to see. The contrast is injected into the bloodstream through an intravenous (IV) line before or during the imaging test and later flushed out in urine. The contrast agent used for primary CNS lymphoma is called gadolinium. You’ll have multiple MRI tests throughout diagnosis and treatment. An MRI should be done early on if your symptoms suggest a brain tumor. It’s also used right after treatment to see how well the treatment worked. You’ll have more MRIs during follow-up to watch for any recurrence or new growth. CT If MRI is unavailable or not recommended for you, you might have a computed tomography (CT or CAT) scan instead. A CT scan uses x-rays to take many images of your body from different angles. A computer then combines the pictures to make a 3D image. After imaging After the MRI or CT scan, your images will be studied by a radiologist, an expert in analyzing images of the nervous system. The radiologist will convey the imaging results to your care team. This information helps your team plan what the next steps of your care should be. If your imaging results suggest a primary CNS lymphoma, the next step is a biopsy. Straps or other devices may help you avoid moving. Biopsy If imaging scans show something that may be a primary CNS lymphoma, your care providers will want to take a sample and test it. A procedure that removes a small piece of tissue for testing is called a biopsy. Getting a biopsy is the only way to be certain that you have cancer. A biopsy also gives your care team clues on how to treat it. The standard method for diagnosing primary CNS lymphoma is a stereotactic biopsy. It’s the recommended procedure when a brain tumor is in a hard-to-reach or vital area. It aims to remove only enough of the tumor to make a diagnosis. A stereotactic biopsy is done by a neurosurgeon in an operating room. First, you’ll be fitted with a frame or several tiny markers around your head to aid the surgery. Next, you’ll be given anesthesia to go to sleep. A small area of your hair will be shaved down to the scalp. The neurosurgeon will then make a little opening in your skull and insert a thin, hollow needle into the brain to remove a sliver of the tumor. A computerized navigation system, connected to MRI or CT imaging, will allow the surgeon to target and remove the sample with a high degree of precision. After removal, the opening in your scalp will be closed with sutures and you’ll be able to go home. What an MRI shows An MRI scan highlights primary CNS lymphoma in the brain. entities.description: Performance Status is a clinical measure of a patient’s ability to perform daily activities, reflecting their overall well-being, general level of fitness, and capacity for self-care. It is commonly evaluated using standardized scales, such as the ECOG (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group) scale, which assigns a score to quantify a person’s functional capability. This assessment is widely used in cancer care, including in the context of follicular lymphoma (FL), where it informs treatment planning and helps guide therapeutic decisions. Performance Status serves as a key indicator for determining the appropriate level of treatment intensity and is also used to assess a patient’s eligibility for clinical trials. By evaluating how well a patient can manage ordinary day-to-day tasks, this metric provides clinicians with essential information to tailor care and predict a patient’s ability to tolerate specific interventions.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Biomarker Testing is a medical procedure used in oncology that analyzes biological molecules—such as DNA mutations, proteins, or other molecular features—found in tumor tissue, biopsy samples, or blood to inform cancer care. Also known as molecular testing or tumor profiling, it is performed to identify specific genetic alterations or protein expressions that indicate the presence or progression of cancer, thereby aiding in diagnosis and prognosis. The testing examines genes or their products to detect mutations and proteins that may suggest effective treatment options, helping to guide decisions on whether a patient is eligible for targeted therapies or immunotherapies.

The scope of biomarker testing is broad, encompassing various cancer types and specific markers. For instance, it is used to guide diagnosis and treatment in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), and to assess risk and aggressiveness in prostate cancer by examining molecular components of biopsy samples. Common biomarkers tested include hormone receptors, HER2, PD-L1, MMR, MSI, TMB, NTRK, RET, p16, and EBV DNA, among others. These tests help determine the presence of specific biological markers that can predict response to particular drugs, thereby fine-tuning treatment plans and improving diagnostic accuracy.

Biomarker testing can be performed on tumor tissue or through liquid biopsies of blood, depending on the clinical need. The results provide critical information on the molecular profile of the cancer, enabling healthcare providers to select the most appropriate and personalized therapeutic approach. By identifying actionable mutations or protein levels, this testing plays a central role in precision medicine, ensuring that patients receive treatments most likely to be effective while avoiding unnecessary interventions.

Family History is a comprehensive record of the health information of an individual's blood relatives, including parents, siblings, children, grandparents, aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews, and half-siblings. This information encompasses the presence of various diseases and health conditions, such as heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, along with the age at which relatives were diagnosed. It serves as a critical tool in clinical practice, used to assess an individual's risk for inherited conditions and to guide healthcare decisions, treatment plans, and preventive care.

The utility of Family History is particularly pronounced in oncology. It is a key risk factor for several types of cancer, including basal cell skin cancer, prostate cancer, thyroid cancer, and bladder cancer. For instance, having a close relative (like a parent or sibling) with prostate or bladder cancer increases an individual's chance of developing the disease. Furthermore, a detailed history of cancer occurrences in family members, including the specific type of cancer and age of onset, is essential for identifying potential hereditary cancer syndromes. This information can prompt healthcare providers to recommend genetic testing and risk assessment to determine if an individual carries a higher genetic predisposition for certain malignancies, such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

Imaging refers to a broad range of diagnostic techniques and tests that create detailed pictures of the inside of the body, used primarily to detect, stage, and monitor various cancers and other conditions. These techniques include computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), PET/CT, ultrasound, and X-rays, among others. In oncology, imaging is essential for finding tumors, such as adrenal tumors, and for visualizing internal structures like the brain, bladder, and surrounding tissues to assess tumor size, location, and spread.

Specifically, imaging plays a critical role in cancer staging, helping to determine the extent of disease and whether surgery is a viable option, as seen in pancreatic cancer and other malignancies. For certain cancers, such as locally advanced cervical cancer, imaging techniques like CT, MRI, PET, and transvaginal ultrasound are used to identify lymph node involvement and detect recurrence or spread. Additionally, imaging is employed to monitor cancer response during chemotherapy and to guide surveillance after treatment, with recommendations varying by cancer type and stage. For example, in anal cancer, yearly imaging for three years is advised for stage II and III cases, while post-recurrence treatment may involve regular CT or MRI scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Overall, imaging is a cornerstone of modern medical diagnosis and management, providing objective, non-invasive visualization to guide clinical decisions across multiple disease contexts.

entities.description: Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive medical imaging technique that uses a powerful magnet, radio waves, and a computer to create detailed, cross-sectional pictures of areas inside the body, including organs, soft tissues, bones, and internal structures. Unlike X-rays or CT scans, MRI does not use ionizing radiation, making it a safe option for repeated imaging. The technique encompasses both closed and open types of machines and can be performed with or without contrast material, which is often administered to enhance the visibility of specific tissues or abnormalities. MRI is widely used to detect, diagnose, and stage various conditions, including cancers, and is particularly valuable for examining soft tissue contrast.

In oncology, MRI plays a critical role in cancer detection, staging, and treatment planning. It is used to assess the depth of tumor invasion and lymph node involvement, notably in rectal cancer staging, and to detect cancer spread in the spine and brain. In addition to the 2 ovaries, this system includes the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina. The ovaries make eggs needed for sexual reproduction. They also release hormones that affect breast growth, body shape, and the menstrual cycle (periods). Each ovary is about the size and shape of a grape. One is on the left side of the uterus and the other is on the right. Each is surrounded by a long, thin tube called a fallopian tube. After an egg is pushed out by the ovary, it is caught by the fallopian tube and travels into the uterus. Here the fetus grows and develops during pregnancy. If the egg is not fertilized, this leads to a period. The uterus and at least 1 ovary and fallopian tube are needed for menstruation and pregnancy. The female reproductive system The female reproductive system includes the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina. Types of ovarian cancer Most ovarian cancers are found in the outer surface of the ovaries, called the epithelium. There are more than 5 types of epithelial ovarian cancer. The most common forms are: High-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC) High-grade endometrioid carcinoma Less common ovarian cancers Rare types of ovarian cancer are called less common ovarian cancers (LCOCs) or less common ovarian histologies (LCOHs). They can start in the epithelium, in tissues that support the ovaries, or in the reproductive (egg) cells of the ovary. Less common epithelial ovarian cancers include: Low-grade serous carcinoma Low-grade endometrioid carcinoma Carcinosarcoma (also called malignant mixed Mullerian tumors) Clear cell carcinoma Mucinous carcinoma Borderline epithelial tumor (also called low malignant potential tumors) Less common non-epithelial ovarian cancers include: Malignant sex-cord stromal tumors Malignant germ cell tumors Primary peritoneal cancer Primary peritoneal cancer forms in the the tissue that lines the abdominal wall and covers the abdominal organs. The treatment information in this guide also applies to primary peritoneal cancer and fallopian tube cancer. How is the type determined? To diagnose ovarian cancer and determine the cancer type, tumor tissue needs to be removed from your body and tested. If surgery is planned first, the tumor and other tissues removed during surgery will be tested. If chemotherapy is planned first, a biopsy will be performed to remove a sample of the tumor. A physician expert called a pathologist determines the type of ovarian cancer by examining the cancerous tissue. The pathologist also determines the cancer grade. The grade is a rating of how abnormal the cancer cells look under a microscope. High-grade cancers grow and spread more quickly than low-grade cancers. The cancer grade is different than the stage. Stages are categories that describe where the cancer has or hasn't spread from the ovary. Surgery is needed in order to know exactly how much cancer is in the body. Testing can provide a best guess of how far the cancer has spread before surgery. Cancer care plan Your treatment team Treatment for ovarian cancer takes a team of experts. When possible, a gynecologic oncologist should perform the initial surgery. This type of doctor is an expert in surgery and chemotherapy for gynecologic cancers. Your care team may also include a medical oncologist. This doctor is an expert in treating cancer with chemotherapy and other medicines. You may also receive care from registered nurses, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, social workers, genetic counselors, sexual health experts, and others. Ask for the names and contact information of your care providers to be included in the treatment plan. Cancer treatment may be improved if your primary care provider is involved. They can help manage other health conditions that may be affected by your cancer treatment. Your treatment plan There isn't one treatment plan that is best for everyone. There is often more than one option, including clinical trials. Clinical trials study the safety and effectiveness of investigational treatments. The treatment that you and your care team agree on should be noted in the treatment plan, along with possible side effects. Keep in mind that your plan may change. Testing may provide new information. Your feelings about treatment may change. Side effects or other health conditions may prompt a change of plan. Key points The ovaries are a pair of grapesized organs in the pelvis. They make hormones and eggs for sexual reproduction. Most ovarian cancers affect the layer of tissue surrounding the ovaries, called the epithelium. High-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC) and high-grade endometrioid carcinoma are the most common types of ovarian tumors. Less common ovarian cancers can start in the epithelium, in tissues that support the ovaries, or in the reproductive (egg) cells of the ovary. Treating ovarian cancer takes a team of experts. Gynecologic oncologists and medical oncologists often work together to plan your treatment. 2 Testing for ovarian cancer Abdominal and pelvic exam Imaging tests Biopsy Family history and genetic testing Nutritional and digestive tract health Blood tests Biomarker testing Key points This chapter describes the testing used to learn more about suspected ovarian cancer, including whether surgery is possible. Ovarian cancer can cause changes in the body that you can feel or notice. But you might not have symptoms until the tumor has grown large or the cancer has spread. Common symptoms include: Feeling bloated Heartburn and indigestion Pain or pressure in the pelvis or belly Trouble eating or feeling full fast Having to urinate often or urgently Pain during sex These symptoms can also be caused by hormonal changes or other common health problems.

Types of PET scans that can be helpful for those with adrenal tumors include FDG-PET and SSTRPET. FDG-PET/CT scan An FDG-PET scan uses a radioactive type of sugar (18-fluorodeoxyglucose) as its tracer. Active cancer cells use sugar faster than normal cells. This will make the cells look brighter in pictures. Many adrenal tumors are not fast-growing and not very bright on FDG-PET scans. FDG-PET scans can help determine if neuroendocrine tumors are becoming more aggressive. Somatostatin helps to control other hormones in the body. SSTRs are found on many different types of cells. A SSTR-PET uses a tracer that binds to these SSTRs. Blood tests Blood tests are used to look for signs of hormone secretion or to see how well you are responding to certain treatments. Biochemical tests Biochemical tests measure substances like hormones in blood, urine, and/or saliva that may be made by the adrenal tumor. Symptoms may be seen when your body makes too much of a hormone. Your doctor may consider these tests if you may have an adrenal tumor or syndromes caused by a tumor. The third type—melanoma—is much less common than the other types but can be more aggressive. Because they do not behave like melanoma, basal cell and squamous cell skin cancers are often referred to as nonmelanoma skin cancers or keratinocyte carcinomas. Cancer that starts in a squamous cell is called a squamous cell carcinoma. Squamous cells are found in the top layer of the skin. They can also be found in other areas of the body, such as the lungs, thyroid, and esophagus. These types are treated differently than cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Squamous cell skin cancers often begin as scaly patches on the skin that can become solid and misshapen. This cancer is also called cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC). This patient guide is about squamous cell skin cancer only. The terms “squamous cell skin cancer” and “CSCC” are used interchangeably throughout this guide. Skin basics Your skin is the largest organ of the body. Skin protects you from invaders (such as microbes), helps control body temperature, and allows the sensations of touch, heat, and cold. Skin has 3 layers: Epidermis is the outermost (top) layer of skin that provides a waterproof barrier and creates skin color (melanin). Dermis contains connective tissue, hair follicles, and sweat glands. Hypodermis (subcutis) is the deepest layer, made up of fat and connective tissue. Skin cancers are often formed in the epidermis. There are 3 main types of cells in the epidermis: Squamous cells: These cells are thin, flat cells that look like fish scales, and are found in the tissue that forms the surface of the skin. Basal cells: These cells are found in the lower part of the epidermis, called the basal cell layer. Basal cells constantly divide to form new cells to replace the squamous cells that wear off of the skin’s surface. As these cells move up in the epidermis, they get flatter, eventually becoming squamous cells. Melanocytes: These cells are found in the top layer of skin. Melanin is produced in the melanocytes. Melanin is responsible for the color of our hair, skin, and eyes. In addition to providing color, melanin also protects our skin from harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays. Risk factors A risk factor is something that increases the chances of getting a disease. For example, smoking cigarettes is a risk factor for developing lung cancer. The major risk factors for squamous cell skin cancer are described next. Sunlight/outdoor tanning Most squamous cell skin cancers are caused by spending too much time in the sun over the course of many years, especially in people who sunburn easily. People with light skin, hair, and eyes who have been in the sun very often throughout their lives are at the highest risk for squamous cell skin cancer. People who work outdoors are also at higher risk. Because longterm sun exposure can lead to squamous cell skin cancer, it is more common in people who have spent more years in the sun. Sun exposure Most squamous cell skin cancers are caused by spending too much time in the sun over a long period of time, frequent tanning, and getting sunburns. Indoor tanning Indoor tanning is a major risk factor for squamous cell skin cancer. Using all types of indoor tanning machines (eg, booths, beds) increases the risk of getting any type of skin cancer. Environmental toxins People who are often exposed to pollutants such as tobacco smoke, exhaust from cars or other vehicles, and arsenic (which can be found in soil, water, and air) can experience skin damage that can lead to squamous cell carcinoma. Ovarian cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of malignant cells in the ovaries, and it can also originate in the fallopian tubes. This condition encompasses various types and subtypes, including high-grade serous carcinoma and high-grade endometrioid carcinoma, and is often linked to genetic factors such as germline mutations, particularly BRCA mutations, as well as Lynch syndrome. The disease may also be associated with a family history that could increase the risk of other cancers, such as prostate cancer.

Diagnosis of ovarian cancer typically involves imaging techniques and biopsy to confirm the presence of cancer cells. A notable challenge is that the disease often presents without symptoms until it reaches advanced stages, making early detection difficult. When symptoms do appear, they are discussed alongside diagnostic and treatment approaches in medical literature.

The condition is staged using a system that ranges from stage 1 to stage 4, with further substages, and treatment recommendations are based on these staging protocols. Standard treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, and maintenance therapy, all of which are described in clinical guidelines. Overall, ovarian cancer is a complex disease with multiple subtypes, genetic associations, and a structured approach to diagnosis, staging, and management.

Head And Neck Cancer is a broad and diverse category of malignancies that arise in the squamous cells lining the mucosal surfaces of the head and neck region. This group encompasses cancers of the oral cavity (including the mouth, jaw, teeth, and gums), the pharynx (throat), the larynx (voice box), and associated glands. As a broader classification, it includes specific subtypes such as throat cancer. The primary risk factors for developing these cancers include the use of tobacco and alcohol, though a subset of these cancers is also caused by the Human Papillomavirus (HPV).

The disease and its treatment can have significant impacts on a patient's quality of life, potentially affecting the health of the jaw, teeth, and gums, and may necessitate dental work prior to the initiation of treatment. Furthermore, cancer therapies for this region can impact fertility. For patients, particularly those with smoking or vaping habits, cessation is deemed essential to maximize the chances of a cure and to minimize the severity of treatment-related side effects.

Mouth Cancer, also known as oral cancer or oral cavity cancer, is a malignant condition that develops in any part of the mouth, including the lips, buccal mucosa (inner cheek lining), tongue, gums, floor of the mouth, hard palate, and retromolar trigone. It is classified as a type of head and neck cancer and most commonly originates in the squamous cells, making it typically a squamous cell carcinoma of the mucosa of the lip and other oral surfaces. The disease is a recognized topic in medical literature and is referenced in resources such as the NCCN (National Comprehensive Cancer Network) guidelines, which provide further information on its management.

Clinically, Mouth Cancer is staged using the TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) system, with stages ranging from 0 to 4. This staging process is crucial as it directly guides treatment decisions, helping clinicians determine the appropriate therapeutic approach based on the extent of the disease. However, from a molecular perspective, testing for this cancer has limited value due to the scarcity of targeted drugs available for its treatment, which contrasts with other cancer types where molecular profiling may offer more actionable therapeutic options. Overall, Mouth Cancer encompasses a range of malignancies within the oral cavity, with its diagnosis, staging, and treatment protocols being well-documented in oncological practice.

Squamous Cell Carcinoma is a type of cancer that arises from squamous cells, which are thin, flat cells found in tissues forming the surface of the skin, mucous membranes, and the lining of various organs and airways. Because these cells are widespread, squamous cell carcinoma can develop in multiple anatomical sites, and its characteristics, prevalence, and staging vary depending on the location.

In the context of lung cancer, squamous cell carcinoma is a subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that originates in the squamous cells lining the bronchi or airways. In the head and neck region, it is the most common type of mouth cancer, arising from the squamous cells lining the mucous membranes inside the mouth, and it is also the most common type of throat cancer, forming in the thin, flat cells of the mucus membranes. For throat cancer, staging information for this type is provided when the tumor tests negative for p16. Additionally, it is the most common type of nasopharyngeal cancer, forming in the squamous cells lining the nasopharynx, and the TNM staging system is specifically applied to this type of nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

Squamous cell carcinoma is also the most common type of cervical cancer, arising from squamous cells in the ectocervix. In the bladder, it represents a less common, non-urothelial type of cancer. Finally, it is the most common type of anal cancer, originating in the squamous cells that form the surface of the skin and other tissues, and it is the focus of certain patient guides for anal cancer. Overall, while the fundamental origin in squamous cells is consistent, the clinical significance, frequency, and management of squamous cell carcinoma are highly dependent on the primary site of the disease.

Bone is a specialized connective tissue that forms the skeleton, characterized as a hard yet living tissue composed of bone cells, collagen, blood vessels, nerves, proteins, vitamins, and minerals. It is light and strong, capable of regrowing and undergoing continuous remodeling, and it also produces hormones. As a dynamic tissue, bone can be damaged by cancer, leading to complications such as calcium release into the body.

In the context of oncology, bone is a frequent and clinically significant site for metastasis across multiple cancer types. It is a common site for distant metastasis in breast cancer, including spread to the spine, and is also a primary target for prostate cancer metastasis, often detected via bone scans. Additionally, bone serves as a common site for metastatic esophageal cancer, cervical cancer, liver cancer, and stomach cancer. When cancer spreads to bone, affected areas may appear as bright spots on imaging scans due to increased tracer absorption, indicating active metastatic lesions.

Metastasis is the biological process by which cancer spreads from its primary, or original, site to other parts of the body. This dissemination occurs when cancer cells travel through the bloodstream or lymphatic system, enabling them to establish new tumors in distant or nearby anatomical locations. The process is a defining characteristic of advanced-stage cancer, as it marks the transition from a localized disease to a systemic one.

The specific destinations for metastatic spread vary depending on the origin of the primary cancer. Common sites of secondary tumor formation include the lymph nodes, lungs, bones, and liver. For instance, metastasis from prostate cancer defines advanced-stage disease, while bladder cancer may spread to lymph nodes, bones, liver, or lungs. In the context of kidney cancer, metastasis refers to the formation of new tumors outside the kidney itself.

Clinically, the presence of metastasis often necessitates further diagnostic procedures, such as a biopsy, to confirm the spread and guide treatment decisions. The formation of these secondary tumors is a critical factor in cancer prognosis, as it indicates that the disease has become more complex and challenging to treat.

As an inherited cancer syndrome, Lynch Syndrome is fundamentally linked to an increased susceptibility to a broad spectrum of cancers, with colon and uterine cancers being the most prominent, followed by ovarian and other extracolonic malignancies.

In clinical practice, histology involves the detailed review of the appearance and cellular composition of tissue samples. This discipline is fundamental to pathology, where it is used to classify cancer subtypes—such as renal cell carcinoma (RCC)—by examining tissue under a microscope. Biomarker Testing is a medical procedure used in oncology that analyzes biological molecules—such as DNA mutations, proteins, or other molecular features—found in tumor tissue, biopsy samples, or blood to inform cancer care. Also known as molecular testing or tumor profiling, it is performed to identify specific genetic alterations or protein expressions that indicate the presence or progression of cancer, thereby aiding in diagnosis and prognosis. The testing examines genes or their products to detect mutations and proteins that may suggest effective treatment options, helping to guide decisions on whether a patient is eligible for targeted therapies or immunotherapies.

The scope of biomarker testing is broad, encompassing various cancer types and specific markers. For instance, it is used to guide diagnosis and treatment in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), and to assess risk and aggressiveness in prostate cancer by examining molecular components of biopsy samples. Common biomarkers tested include hormone receptors, HER2, PD-L1, MMR, MSI, TMB, NTRK, RET, p16, and EBV DNA, among others. These tests help determine the presence of specific biological markers that can predict response to particular drugs, thereby fine-tuning treatment plans and improving diagnostic accuracy.

Biomarker testing can be performed on tumor tissue or through liquid biopsies of blood, depending on the clinical need. The results provide critical information on the molecular profile of the cancer, enabling healthcare providers to select the most appropriate and personalized therapeutic approach. By identifying actionable mutations or protein levels, this testing plays a central role in precision medicine, ensuring that patients receive treatments most likely to be effective while avoiding unnecessary interventions.

A tumor is an abnormal mass or growth of tissue that arises from the uncontrolled overgrowth of cells, and it can be either benign (non-cancerous) or malignant (cancerous). In the context of cancer, a tumor specifically refers to the primary cancerous mass, which is a key element in staging and treatment planning. Tumors can develop in various parts of the body, including lymph nodes, the prostate, the bladder, bones, the throat, and the ovaries, where they may present as solid or fluid-filled masses. Their size is often measured in centimeters or millimeters, and this measurement, along with the extent of local invasion into nearby structures, is used to assign a T score in cancer staging systems. For example, primary bone tumors are staged based on size and location, while throat and bladder tumors are assessed for their potential to invade deeper tissue layers or spread. Tumors may be detected as irregular or hardened areas during physical examination, such as in the prostate, or identified through medical procedures. Biopsy samples are commonly taken from tumors to determine whether they are cancerous, and in many cases, tumors can be surgically removed. Overall, the term tumor encompasses a wide range of abnormal growths, with its clinical significance largely determined by its benign or malignant nature, size, location, and potential for invasion or metastasis.

Cancer is a broad class of diseases characterized by uncontrolled or abnormal cell growth, where cells divide out of control due to genetic changes, and can invade nearby tissues, spread, and harm the body. This condition can affect various parts of the body, may run in families, and encompasses many specific types, including chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), primary CNS lymphoma, and breast cancer, among others. Cancer presents in various stages, including metastatic and numbered stages, and can cause significant physical effects, such as bone damage, as well as emotional and psychological distress for patients. The disease can also impact fertility, often requiring medical treatment that addresses both the cancer and its side effects.

Diagnosis and management of cancer rely heavily on a range of medical techniques, including various imaging methods and biopsy procedures, which are used to detect, characterize, and monitor the disease. Treatment approaches are diverse and are discussed extensively in medical contexts, aiming to control or eliminate the abnormal cell growth. Given its complexity, cancer is a central subject of medical texts, which explore its testing, treatment, and overall impact on patients' lives.

These techniques include computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), PET/CT, ultrasound, and X-rays, among others. In oncology, imaging is essential for finding tumors, such as adrenal tumors, and for visualizing internal structures like the brain, bladder, and surrounding tissues to assess tumor size, location, and spread.

For example, in anal cancer, yearly imaging for three years is advised for stage II and III cases, while post-recurrence treatment may involve regular CT or MRI scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Overall, imaging is a cornerstone of modern medical diagnosis and management, providing objective, non-invasive visualization to guide clinical decisions across multiple disease contexts.

Primary CNS Lymphoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that originates in lymphocytes within the central nervous system (CNS). It most commonly affects the brain, often developing deep within brain tissue, but can also occur in the spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, and the eyes. The disease can spread within the nervous system but rarely metastasizes to other areas of the body. Diagnosis typically requires a biopsy and imaging tests to confirm the presence of the malignancy.

As a specific type of lymphoma confined to the CNS, it is the subject of various therapeutic approaches discussed in medical literature. Treatment options for this condition are actively explored, with multiple therapies being considered or applied to manage the disease. The cancer's aggressive nature and its location within the CNS make it a challenging condition to treat, necessitating specialized medical intervention.

Squamous Cell Skin Cancer, also referred to as CSCC, is a type of cancer that arises from squamous cells in the skin. It is the second most common form of skin cancer and is highly treatable, particularly when detected early. The condition is most often caused by cumulative sun exposure, and it can also develop in areas of skin that have been damaged by ultraviolet radiation. In addition to sun-damaged skin, CSCC can form in scars, chronic wounds, old burns, or other areas of prior skin injury; cases arising in such contexts may be more challenging to treat.

The disease has the potential to spread, or metastasize, to lymph nodes and other parts of the body, which underscores the importance of timely intervention. Treatment options for squamous cell skin cancer include topical therapies and surgical removal, with the choice of approach depending on the lesion's characteristics and location. The condition encompasses various subtypes, and risk factors—such as history of skin damage or chronic inflammation—are important considerations in its development and management. Overall, while CSCC is a serious malignancy, its prognosis is generally favorable with appropriate and prompt care.

The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are a comprehensive set of patient-friendly guidelines published by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN), a nonprofit alliance of leading cancer centers. These guidelines translate the expert consensus of the NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology into plain-language explanations, designed to help people with cancer, their families, and caregivers understand current care recommendations. The guidelines are based on the latest research and practices at leading cancer centers, providing trusted, up-to-date information on cancer treatment, testing, staging, and side effects.

These resources cover a wide range of cancer types, including squamous cell skin cancer, melanoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, acute myeloid leukemia (AML), acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), rectal cancer, anal cancer, bone cancer, and certain lymphomas, as well as topics like adolescent and young adult cancer. They also address specific concerns such as immunotherapy side effects and fertility and family planning for cancer patients. The guidelines aim to empower patients to make informed, shared decisions with their care team by clearly explaining their treatment options and what to expect.

The NCCN Guidelines for Patients are accessible in multiple formats, including online at NCCN.org/patientguidelines and through the NCCN Patient Guides for Cancer app. They are also available as printed books. The NCCN encourages users to provide feedback through surveys to help improve the guidelines. Overall, these guidelines serve as a vital educational resource, bridging the gap between complex medical information and patient understanding, ensuring individuals are well-informed participants in their own cancer care journey.

entities.description: Prostate Cancer is a disease in which cells in the prostate gland grow out of control, and it is one of the most common types of cancer. The condition can be early-stage (localized) or advanced-stage (metastatic), with the latter occurring when cancer spreads outside the prostate to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes and bones, through a process called metastasis. Prostate cancer is often slow-growing and asymptomatic in its early stages, contributing to high survival rates when detected early. Risk factors for developing the disease include age, family history, genetic factors, race, and lifestyle. Detection and risk assessment involve various tests, including PSA (prostate-specific antigen) levels, biopsy, and grading, and the disease often requires staging and treatment. The condition is also a focus of risk assessment and genetic testing discussions, as it is characterized by the presence of prostate cancer cells and abnormal cell growth within the gland.

Bladder cancer is a disease in which malignant cells form in the tissues of the bladder, most commonly originating in the urothelial cells that line the inside of the organ. This abnormal cell growth can be classified into several clinical categories, including non-muscle-invasive, muscle-invasive, and metastatic forms, reflecting the extent to which the cancer has spread within or beyond the bladder wall. The disease is most frequently diagnosed in adults aged 55 and older, and its development is influenced by risk factors such as smoking and genetic predisposition.

Diagnosis of bladder cancer typically involves a range of tests and procedures aimed at detecting the presence and extent of the malignancy. The condition is often identified through imaging, urine tests, and biopsy, with the specific diagnostic approach tailored to the individual case. Once diagnosed, the cancer is staged and graded to determine its aggressiveness and spread, which directly informs the treatment strategy.

Treatment for bladder cancer is highly individualized, depending on the stage and grade of the tumor, the patient’s overall health, and their personal preferences. Options may include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, or a combination of these approaches. Given the complexity of the disease, management often requires a multidisciplinary care team, including urologists, oncologists, and other specialists, to coordinate comprehensive care. The goal of treatment is to remove or destroy the cancer while preserving bladder function whenever possible, though more advanced or recurrent cases may necessitate more aggressive interventions.

Family History is a comprehensive record of the health information of an individual's blood relatives, including parents, siblings, children, grandparents, aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews, and half-siblings. This information encompasses the presence of various diseases and health conditions, such as heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, along with the age at which relatives were diagnosed. It serves as a critical tool in clinical practice, used to assess an individual's risk for inherited conditions and to guide healthcare decisions, treatment plans, and preventive care.

The utility of Family History is particularly pronounced in oncology. It is a key risk factor for several types of cancer, including basal cell skin cancer, prostate cancer, thyroid cancer, and bladder cancer. For instance, having a close relative (like a parent or sibling) with prostate or bladder cancer increases an individual's chance of developing the disease. Furthermore, a detailed history of cancer occurrences in family members, including the specific type of cancer and age of onset, is essential for identifying potential hereditary cancer syndromes. This information can prompt healthcare providers to recommend genetic testing and risk assessment to determine if an individual carries a higher genetic predisposition for certain malignancies, such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

Metastasis is the biological process by which cancer spreads from its primary, or original, site to other parts of the body. This dissemination occurs when cancer cells travel through the bloodstream or lymphatic system, enabling them to establish new tumors in distant or nearby anatomical locations. The process is a defining characteristic of advanced-stage cancer, as it marks the transition from a localized disease to a systemic one.

The specific destinations for metastatic spread vary depending on the origin of the primary cancer. Common sites of secondary tumor formation include the lymph nodes, lungs, bones, and liver. For instance, metastasis from prostate cancer defines advanced-stage disease, while bladder cancer may spread to lymph nodes, bones, liver, or lungs. In the context of kidney cancer, metastasis refers to the formation of new tumors outside the kidney itself.

Clinically, the presence of metastasis often necessitates further diagnostic procedures, such as a biopsy, to confirm the spread and guide treatment decisions. The formation of these secondary tumors is a critical factor in cancer prognosis, as it indicates that the disease has become more complex and challenging to treat.

Prostate Cancer is a disease in which cells in the prostate gland grow out of control, and it is one of the most common types of cancer. The condition can be early-stage (localized) or advanced-stage (metastatic), with the latter occurring when cancer spreads outside the prostate to other parts of the body, such as lymph nodes and bones, through a process called metastasis. Prostate cancer is often slow-growing and asymptomatic in its early stages, contributing to high survival rates when detected early. Risk factors for developing the disease include age, family history, genetic factors, race, and lifestyle. Biopsy is a medical procedure that involves the removal of a sample of tissue, cells, or fluid from the body for examination, typically by a pathologist, to diagnose cancer and determine tumor histology. It is used to confirm the presence of cancer, identify its type, and guide treatment decisions. The procedure is essential for diagnosing various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, adrenal tumors, follicular lymphoma, ovarian cancer, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, DCIS, primary CNS lymphoma, thyroid cancer, bone cancer, brain tumors, bladder cancer, and anal cancer. Biopsies can be performed using different techniques, such as fine-needle aspiration, core needle biopsy, or surgical removal, and may be guided by imaging methods like ultrasound or CT. In some cases, a biopsy is performed during initial surgery, such as for ovarian cancer, or before chemotherapy if recommended. For prostate cancer, a biopsy is often decided after PSA test and digital rectal exam results, and the procedure can temporarily raise PSA levels. A biopsy may also be necessary before starting steroid therapy, as in the case of primary CNS lymphoma. The procedure is the only way to definitively confirm cancer in many cases, and it can also be used for staging, such as in clinical staging, or to confirm cancer progression. Specific types include bone marrow aspirate and biopsy for follicular lymphoma, endometrial biopsy, and Pap test. A biopsy is a key diagnostic tool that removes a small piece of tissue or tumor for laboratory testing, ensuring an accurate diagnosis and informing subsequent treatment plans.

Blood Tests are laboratory procedures performed on samples of blood to evaluate a patient’s overall health, detect abnormalities, and assess organ function. These medical tests are frequently documented in medical records and binders, serving as a foundational tool for diagnosing and monitoring a wide range of conditions, particularly various types of cancer. By analyzing blood components and chemicals, these tests can reveal signs of disease, measure how well organs are working, and identify specific markers or irregularities that guide clinical decision-making.

In the context of oncology, Blood Tests play a critical role across multiple cancer types. They are routine in cases of small cell lung cancer (SCLC), where results may be abnormal, and are integral to the diagnostic workup for esophageal cancer, Hodgkin lymphoma, and follicular lymphoma, where results help guide treatment plans. For suspected ovarian cancer, tests typically include a complete blood count (CBC), chemistry profile, liver function tests, and tumor marker tests. Similarly, for pancreatic cancer, these tests aid in diagnosis and management, while for primary CNS lymphoma, they help assess the condition. In leukemias like acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), blood tests are used to diagnose, monitor, and direct treatment strategies. For thyroid cancer, they measure specific substances such as TSH, thyroglobulin (Tg), and Tg antibodies to track disease status.

Beyond initial diagnosis, Blood Tests are essential for ongoing patient care. They are ordered as needed to monitor health and cancer status during chemotherapy, and they help establish the extent of cancer spread for treatment planning. Specific tests, including CBC, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, and liver function tests, are used to check for cancer recurrence and to evaluate organ function over time. Additionally, these tests are part of general health checks and are crucial for diagnosing and planning treatment for liver cancer. Overall, Blood Tests provide objective data on blood markers and health indicators, making them indispensable for detecting disease, assessing organ performance, and guiding therapeutic decisions across numerous medical scenarios.

Blood Stem Cells, also known as hematopoietic stem cells, are early, immature blood-forming cells located primarily in the bone marrow, including the red marrow. They serve as the foundational origin for all types of blood cells, possessing the unique ability to self-renew and differentiate through various maturation stages into red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets. These cells multiply and mature to maintain the body’s blood supply. Additionally, Blood Stem Cells are identified as the likely cellular origin of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML), as they give rise to myeloid progenitor cells, which are implicated in the disease’s development.

Cervical Cancer is a malignant disease characterized by the abnormal and uncontrolled growth of cells in the tissues of the cervix, the lower part of the uterus connecting to the vagina. It is a common cancer of the female reproductive system and is almost always caused by a persistent infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease often originates in the transformation zone of the cervix, where the cells are particularly susceptible to HPV-related changes. Cervical cancer shares a strong etiological link with anal cancer, as both are frequently driven by HPV; consequently, a history of cervical cancer increases the risk of developing anal cancer.

The disease presents in several histological forms, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and adenosquamous carcinoma. Clinically, cervical cancer can be classified as locally advanced or metastatic, and its progression is formally staged using the FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) system. The stage of the disease at diagnosis is a critical factor in determining the appropriate treatment approach, which varies according to the extent of the cancer. As a significant health concern, cervical cancer is frequently the subject of clinical discussions regarding its management, treatment options, and therapeutic considerations.

Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment modality that uses drugs to kill cancer cells, typically by targeting fast-dividing or rapidly growing cells. As a systemic therapy, it works throughout the body, with drugs traveling via the bloodstream to reach cells in various locations. It is often administered intravenously, either as an infusion or injection, but can also be given orally, intraperitoneally, or directly into the bladder, depending on the cancer type. Chemotherapy is frequently delivered in cycles, allowing the body time to recover between treatments. It can be used as a primary treatment, a standard of care for certain cancers like acute myeloid leukemia (AML), primary CNS lymphoma, and high-grade gliomas, or as part of a combined approach with other therapies, such as radiation (chemoradiation) or immune checkpoint inhibitors.

The application of chemotherapy varies by cancer type and stage. It may be given before surgery (neoadjuvant) to shrink tumors, after surgery (adjuvant) based on disease stage, or as the main treatment for advanced or metastatic cancers, including ovarian, anal, prostate, and perianal cancers. For certain conditions, such as mediastinal gray zone lymphoma or anaplastic thyroid cancer, it is a common or necessary treatment, though it is not highly effective against most thyroid cancers. In stem cell rescue procedures, high-dose chemotherapy is used to destroy lymphoma cells and bone marrow stem cells. Specific drug examples include platinum-based agents like cisplatin and carboplatin, as well as capecitabine and paclitaxel.

Because chemotherapy targets all fast-dividing cells, it can also harm healthy cells, leading to side effects such as nausea, vomiting, fatigue, diarrhea, hair loss, mouth sores, fever, infection, tingling or numbness, and rash. Long-term side effects may include other cancers, heart disease, and infertility, as the treatment can affect fertility. Chemotherapy is considered a non-hormone therapy and is a cornerstone of systemic cancer treatment, though its effectiveness and side effects depend on the specific drugs used and the individual patient's condition.

Anal Cancer is a disease characterized by the abnormal growth of cells in the tissues of the anus, which includes the anal canal and the perianal region. It is an uncommon cancer of the digestive system, most often starting in the squamous cells lining the anal canal, and is frequently caused by an infection with the human papillomavirus (HPV). The disease is staged from precancerous conditions to stage IV, based on tumor size, lymph node involvement, and the presence of metastasis, and it can spread to lymph nodes and other organs. Various types of anal cancer exist, with squamous cell carcinoma being a primary form, and the condition can be either non-metastatic or metastatic.

Treatment for Anal Cancer typically involves a multidisciplinary team of digestive health experts and commonly includes chemoradiation, though surgery and immunotherapy are also viable options depending on the case. The disease has several risk factors and presents with various symptoms, and its treatment can lead to a range of side effects. Management of the disease also encompasses discussions on clinical trials and survivorship, as it is a focus of patient guidelines. While considered a rare cancer, its association with HPV and its distinct staging and treatment pathways make it a specific and serious oncological condition.

Radiation therapy is a medical treatment that uses high-energy radiation, such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons, to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is a localized treatment, meaning it affects a specific area of the body. The therapy is typically administered in daily sessions over several weeks, with each session lasting between 30 and 60 minutes, and is often used alone or in combination with other treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, or systemic therapy.

This treatment is applied to a wide range of cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), prostate cancer (both early and advanced stages), primary CNS lymphoma (including in the eyes, via whole-brain radiation therapy or focused eye treatment), chordoma, glioma, and anal cancer. For some cancers, such as anal cancer, it is a primary initial treatment, often combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation). In other cases, it is recommended when surgery is not an option, as an adjuvant therapy after surgery, or as a main treatment for unresectable tumors.

While effective, radiation therapy carries potential side effects. Short-term effects can include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, and tiredness. Long-term or late-onset side effects may include vision problems, cataracts, damage to the perineum, and effects on endocrine glands and hearing when treating the head and neck. It can also cause infertility. Furthermore, prior exposure to radiation therapy is a known risk factor for developing small cell lung cancer (SCLC). The specific delivery methods include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and brachytherapy.

entities.description:
Radiation therapy is a medical treatment that uses high-energy radiation, such as x-rays, gamma rays, electrons, photons, or protons, to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. It is a localized treatment, meaning it affects a specific area of the body. The therapy is typically administered in daily sessions over several weeks, with each session lasting between 30 and 60 minutes, and is often used alone or in combination with other treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, or systemic therapy.

This treatment is applied to a wide range of cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), prostate cancer (both early and advanced stages), primary CNS lymphoma (including in the eyes, via whole-brain radiation therapy or focused eye treatment), chordoma, glioma, and anal cancer. For some cancers, such as anal cancer, it is a primary initial treatment, often combined with chemotherapy (chemoradiation). In other cases, it is recommended when surgery is not an option, as an adjuvant therapy after surgery, or as a main treatment for unresectable tumors.

While effective, radiation therapy carries potential side effects. Short-term effects can include skin rash, problems swallowing, dry mouth, thick saliva, changes in taste, and tiredness. Long-term or late-onset side effects may include vision problems, cataracts, damage to the perineum, and effects on endocrine glands and hearing when treating the head and neck. It can also cause infertility. Furthermore, prior exposure to radiation therapy is a known risk factor for developing small cell lung cancer (SCLC). The specific delivery methods include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) and brachytherapy.

Squamous Cell Skin Cancer, also referred to as CSCC, is a type of cancer that arises from squamous cells in the skin. It is the second most common form of skin cancer and is highly treatable, particularly when detected early. The condition is most often caused by cumulative sun exposure, and it can also develop in areas of skin that have been damaged by ultraviolet radiation. In addition to sun-damaged skin, CSCC can form in scars, chronic wounds, old burns, or other areas of prior skin injury; cases arising in such contexts may be more challenging to treat.

The disease has the potential to spread, or metastasize, to lymph nodes and other parts of the body, which underscores the importance of timely intervention. Treatment options for squamous cell skin cancer include topical therapies and surgical removal, with the choice of approach depending on the lesion's characteristics and location. The condition encompasses various subtypes, and risk factors—such as history of skin damage or chronic inflammation—are important considerations in its development and management. Overall, while CSCC is a serious malignancy, its prognosis is generally favorable with appropriate and prompt care.

Systemic Therapy is a broad category of cancer treatment that uses drugs or other substances to reach and affect cancer cells throughout the body, rather than targeting a single localized area. These therapies are typically administered intravenously or orally, allowing the medicine to travel through the bloodstream to reach cells in any part of the body. This approach is used to treat various cancers, including basal cell skin cancer, acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), Ewing sarcoma, metastatic cervical cancer, and bladder cancer, among others. Systemic therapy can be employed as a primary treatment, as an initial therapy, or before or after surgery (neoadjuvant or adjuvant settings), and may also be used as maintenance therapy to prevent recurrence.

The main types of systemic therapy include chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy.
